In PERAK, the State Disaster Management Committee (JPBN) Secretariat reported that the Larut, Matang, and Selama district has been hit by floods again, with the relief centre (PPS) at Sekolah Kebangsaan (SK) Simpang housing the highest number of victims, totalling 282 people.

This is followed by the PPS at Dewan Orang Ramai (DOR) Sungai Relong (93 people), Masjid Ali Rouse Kampung Ulu Sepetang (91), Dewan Changkat Larah (73), SK Batu Hampar (71), DOR Kampung Simpang Halt (59), SK Matang Gelugor (58), Dewan Serbaguna Taman Kaya (56), SK Matang (49), Masjid Al Wusta (41), Masjid Al Hidayah (25) and DOR Air Kuning, Asam Kumbang (13).

Meanwhile, in SELANGOR, 1,371 victims from 362 families remain sheltered at six PPS in the Kuala Selangor district this morning, compared to 1,399 people from 370 families yesterday evening.

According to the InfoBencana portal of the Social Welfare Department (JKM), the PPS at SK Parit Mahang accommodates the highest number of evacuees, 399 people, followed by SK Dato’ Maharaja Lela (396), Sekolah Rendah Agama (SRA) Bukit Kuching (280), DOR Bukit Kuching Tengah (116), Kafa Integrasi Hidayah Bukit Cherakah (114), and SRA Batu 8 Ijok (66).

In PENANG, 95 evacuees from 26 families have been relocated to the Village Community Management Council (MPKK) hall in Sungai Kechil, Nibong Tebal, after their homes were hit by floods following several hours of heavy rain last night. The affected areas include Jalan Sekolah and Kampung Sethu.

Yesterday, Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said negotiations on the South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) were in their final stage, with provisional agreement reached on about 80 per cent of the draft.
She said the negotiations would continue beyond the end-2026 target and into 2027, under Singapore’s Asean chairmanship.

432f025c9a36a30a: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 16 — US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China yesterday, saying this was more important than ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged spy for Beijing.

Speaking on Fox News Sunday Morning Futures three days after Huang resigned, Bessent said he wants to know if Nvidia used shell companies to dodge US restrictions and sell its most powerful chips to China.

But late yesterday, tech tycoon Elon Musk and several other Silicon Valley leaders added their signatures to more than 165,000 others on an open letter demanding that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.”
The United States forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, hoping to stay ahead of the Chinese in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
In late 2025, President Donald Trump did authorize sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese — but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.
“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said.
“What’s more important here,” he said, “is to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions.”
Bessent alluded to companies linked to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data centre company that Huang’s alleged lover Alice Huang once worked for.
“And who knew? Because I mean, these shell companies were obvious. They were being investigated. And did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?”
Of Alice Huang, he said: “It doesn’t matter to me whether she’s a spy or not. You know, Jensen’s foibles are his foibles.”
Investigation deadline

Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days, and said the company needed “a dramatic shake-up,” which should include looking “outside” for its next chief.
The United States suspects Megaspeed helped Chinese firms get around US export controls by buying Nvidia chips for its data centers in Southeast Asia, then routing them to China.
The Justice Department is carrying out a criminal probe.
Nvidia late last month said it had investigated these allegations last year and refuted them.
The Financial Times has reported that four federal agencies pushed to have Megaspeed blacklisted by the Commerce Department run by Howard Lutnick, but the department did not do so.
“Many other departments were pushing for this, and Commerce had the pen,” Bessent said, repeating remarks he made Friday that suggest fissures in the Trump administration on this issue.

Jensen Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify in one session before representatives of three House of Representatives committees — Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and a special committee focusing on China — Republican Congressman John Moolenaar, the chairman of that select committee, said yesterday on CBS. He said no date has been set yet.

“And we think that’s going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, also to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia’s philosophy,” Moolenaar said.
On Friday, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.
Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor, the company said earlier this week.
The end of Huang’s 33-year-long run at the helm of Nvidia sent its stock spiraling.
When trading closed on Friday, the stock was down more than 12 per cent over the week, wiping approximately US$573 billion (RM2.3 trillion) off its market value.
Nvidia is due to publish its quarterly report tomorrow. — AFP
707a2a0dade722bd: NOVEMBER 16 — The last time I walked into one of those all-purpose stores (where they sell anything and everything), guess what was the #1 merchandise being promoted?
Squishies. Of any and every kind.
There were durians, croissants, houses, dumplings, soaps, books, bananas, cheeses, breads, etc.
It looks like there isn’t a single thing on Earth (especially our kitchens) which can’t be turned into a foam- or oil- or gel-filled fidget one can squeeze ad infinitum.

In the United States, squishy toy sales hit about US$297 million (RM1.21 billion) in the first half of 2026 — roughly four times that of the prior year — with unit sales nearly doubling to approximately 58.6 million.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
In the United States, squishy toy sales hit about US$297 million (RM1.21 billion) in the first half of 2026. — Unsplash pic
Even if this should turn out eventually to be a fad, for the time being it’s not a minor market glitch. Something’s happening for real.
Heck, I’ve already bought at least two squishies for my family. A huge Cheddar squishy and a “drop” of coconut oil (or maybe it is just a huge bubble filled with coconut oil, I can’t tell).
So what’s happening? Why the sudden demand of these weird-looking high-touch toys?

Well, my guess is as good as yours. But based on my brief experience with these toys, there’s certainly a minor tactile cum sensory utility involved. I won’t say I crave the sensation of squeezing a Squishmallow but I certainly feel something when I try to crush, flatten and even pound that Clayface-looking i-Bloom banana. I can even imagine this is how kneading roti canai dough feels like!

Some psychologists say that because the average squishy gives predictable tactile feedback — you squeeze, the shape changes, it slowly returns — this is a simple cause-effect loop that can provide mini-relief from abstract worries and a small sense of control (and don’t we all crave that nowadays?).

Even for this aspect, users’ preferences vary. Some enjoy toys with “zero bounce-back” (or “no rebound” or “non-resilient”) features i.e. the plastic durian stays more or less crumpled after you, uh, crumple it. It takes a while to regain its original shape.
Guys like me, on the other hand, want to see my squishy resume its shape as soon as possible after I slam it against my desk or slap it between my hands.

Not unlike Labubu and mobile gaming, squishy toys reflect how the market glories in what could be called the “kidult” sector i.e. adult consumers who enjoy and collect media, toys, and activities typically associated with children or adolescents.
Adults can be said to be kids who can no longer afford to act like kids. But hey if we grown-ups can still obtain a simple pleasure from a kid-like toy why the heck not?
Squishies offer simple, low-cost relief in an age of rising stress and growing concerns (about everything from inflation or AI catastrophe).

Limited editions, colour variants, and “hunts” add collector appeal. Tiktok and other short-video platforms complete the marketing loop by blasting thousands of cute squishy videos to our tired workaholic eyes.
It’s no wonder these products are selling like (literal, squeezable) hotcakes.
* This is the personal opinion of the columnist.

4db6a0c5379d7028: JOHOR BAHRU, Nov 16 — Two people were killed, and two others were injured in an accident involving three vehicles at Kilometre 52.5 of the Senai-Desaru Expressway (SDE), heading towards Desaru, early today.

He said upon arrival, firefighters found that the accident involved a Proton X70, a Proton Persona and a Toyota Unser, with five people involved.
The two fatalities were identified as a 58-year-old man travelling in the Proton X70 and a 26-year-old woman in the Proton Persona.

936348b61b0e5836: BERLIN: The crisis in Germany's skilled trades sector is worsening despite more favourable growth forecasts, German Press Agency (dpa) reported, citing the president of the German Confederation of Skilled Trades on Sunday.
"Our business climate index is at the level of the coronavirus pandemic, investment has fallen to the level of the financial crisis," Jorg Dittrich told newspapers of the Funke Media Group.

He warned that, if nothing was done to counter this, the trade sector would "lose between 70,000 and 80,000 jobs a year." He added that more than 150,000 jobs had already been lost in the sector over the past two years.
Skilled trades are a key part of the German economy and cover jobs ranging from construction and electrical positions to food production and health and personal care jobs.
"Many business owners lack confidence, others simply lack the financial means. And then they shut up shop," Dittrich said.
The sector was experiencing a "silent death of businesses." The high cost of living was also putting skilled trades workers under pressure.
"Anyone who spends a lot at the petrol station is more inclined to think twice about having one fewer haircut or buying one fewer cake or piece of jewellery," he added.
To halt the trend, Dittrich called for a reduction in non-wage labour costs and for the coalition to push through its promised electricity tax cut for the trades.
He warned that successful vocational training programmes were at risk of being cut.
"It is undignified how the trades sector is being treated."

7f4dde97263ceb68: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 16 — Xiao long bao, or little dragon dumplings are the most recognisable soup dumplings popularised by the Taiwan restaurant chain Din Tai Fung.
They are believed to have been invented in 1870 by Huang Mingxian, who came up with the idea of including jellied stock with minced pork wrapped in dough, which created soup when steamed.
Din Tai Fung's small dumplings are crafted with obsessive precision: each dumpling weighs 21 grams, with the pork filling at 16 grams, the skin at five grams and pleated with 18 folds.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The restaurant has diners throughout the day for its dumplings and solo meals — Picture by Lee Khang Yi

This small shop inside Taman Bukit Anggerik may not be as analytical or precise with its xiao long bao but its thin, firm skin hugs the meat filling and there's lots of soup, which many regard as the criteria for a good xiao long bao.
You first notice these dumplings are huge compared to the dainty ones from the Taiwanese chain restaurant that one can easily pop whole into your mouth.
Its folds aren't pinched evenly nor are they tiny pleats but there's no massive excess dough at the top that most makers fail to remove, which often leaves you with a hard bite of dough.

Believe me, having gone through a few cooking classes where I learned to make pleats in dough, it's a hard task to master since each fold needs to be even and the dough must properly cover the filling well.
Now comes the moment of truth: can this dumpling's thin skin hold the soup and filling when you lift it with a pair of chopsticks?
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The moment of truth for a ‘xiao long bao’ is whether you can hold it up with your chopsticks — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
I cautiously use a spoon first just in case it falls or bursts open and ruins my photo.
The dumpling holds its form on the spoon even though it does not fit on it.
As I nibble the thin skin, the clear broth spills out and you slowly eat it with the fluffy filling, which has a magic ratio of finely diced fat and meat.
This dumpling comes with a caveat, though: although the soup is plentiful, the clear broth has a pretty light flavour that needs more vinegar and fresh ginger shreds.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The steamed dumplings use a thin skin that is slightly pinched to hold the pork and chives filling together — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Next was the chopsticks moment and this dumpling aced the test.

The soup weighed it down, letting it droop with the threat of bursting all of its liquid onto the steamer but it held on, a marvel of how the thin yet firm skin kept its promise of keeping the soup intact.
You can also customise the size of your order, with portions ranging from three dumplings for RM8 to six dumplings for RM14.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
One order comes with two types of filling: one with pork and cabbage and another with pork and chives — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
They also offer dumplings — a mix of pork with cabbage or pork with chives — served steamed or fried.
The skin used is rolled much thinner than others and gently pressed together to close the edges, though sometimes you see a gap because in haste, it's not closed properly.
Inside, the filling is soft and juicy, requiring little embellishment to distract you from its natural flavours.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Fried dumplings may look unappealing but the thin skin is shatteringly crispy — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
When fried, the thin skins become shatteringly crispy and even more enjoyable.
The dumplings can be ordered as four for RM8 or eight for RM14.
Since the dumplings aren't a main meal, there are bowls of noodles (soup or dry) and even dishes like pork trotter with rice to fill your stomach.
Handmade noodles have a curly, bouncy texture that pairs with the minced meat topping, with a choice of char siu or siew yoke and a fried egg that range from RM9 to RM12, depending on your choices.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Supplement the meal with an order of handmade noodles with minced meat, a fried egg and ‘char siu’ — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
There are also rice noodles that can be enjoyed with soup or the meat topping.
Many of their regulars are residents of the neighbouring area who will pre-order their food and pick it up to enjoy in the comfort of their homes.
Restoran Guangzhou 88
Taman Bukit Anggerik,
Cheras, Kuala Lumpur.
Open daily: 7.30am to 5pm
* This is an independent review where the writer paid for the meal.

843896768419b8c6: TEHRAN, Nov 16 — Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said yesterday that a supertanker carrying over two million barrels of oil had sunk after it struck a mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz.
The ship was one of two that hit mines while transiting the vital trade corridor, the Guards said, but there was no independent confirmation of the incidents.
Since the outbreak of the Middle East war in late February, Tehran has heavily restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, insisting vessels use routes authorised by the Islamic republic.
It has regularly targeted ships that transit without its authorisation.
The United States has in response imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and helped tankers travel the strait, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil.
The American military recently claimed to have cleared all mines from the main routes through the waterway.

“Over the past few hours, two oil tankers travelling along an unauthorised route in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz struck naval mines, resulting in massive explosions and fire,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement carried by state TV.
“One of these vessels — a super tanker carrying over two million barrels of crude oil — sank in the southern waters of the Persian Gulf,” the statement added.
It did not specify the names or origins of the tankers.
In recent weeks Tehran has made multiple announcements saying ships had caught fire in the strait, often claiming they struck mines.

US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the region, has been supporting ships traversing the waterway and said last month that it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer.

A British maritime monitor on Sunday said it was aware of a report by Indian shipping authorities of an attack on a tanker in the Gulf, but it was unclear if it was the same incident as the one announced by Iran’s Guards.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre said the damage and environmental impact were unknown but the crew were safe. — AFP

930d58decab90eda: PETALING JAYA: A Bersatu leader has defended the party from criticism following its poor showing in the Melaka polls, saying it remains relevant to Malay-Muslim voters who prioritise integrity and their principles, and reject corruption.

Bersatu information chief Tun Faisal Ismail Aziz said the party also remained a relevant option for Malays who reject betrayal, slander, abuse of power and leaders who use religion for political interests.
He denied that the party had lost influence among Malay voters, saying its candidate in Pantai Kundor polled over 6,000 votes, or 40.8%.
"Meanwhile in Lendu, Bemban and Sungai Udang, Bersatu received more than 2,000 votes. Why were Malay voters still voting for Bersatu in the Melaka polls?
"They want assemblymen capable of solving their problems. They aren't influenced by the Malay-Muslim narratives played up by Barisan Nasional and PAS.

"This segment of voters sees the Malay-Muslim narrative as a mere tool to garner political support and power while shifting attention from the weaknesses of the Umno-led Melaka government," he said in a statement.

Tun Faisal was responding to political analyst Tawfik Yaakub, who said Bersatu's wipeout in the Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka elections showed that the party was no longer relevant to Malay voters.
Tawfik, of Universiti Malaya, said Bersatu needed to execute drastic changes across the party and fortify its organisation if it hoped to retain relevance in the national political arena.
Five of Bersatu's seven candidates lost their deposits in the Melaka polls. In the Negeri Sembilan election, only one of its 24 candidates kept their election deposit.
Tun Faisal acknowledged that Bersatu needed a "game changer" to woo voters, but insisted that the party would stick to its principles and work hard to attract Malaysians.
"The number of voters who are with Bersatu right now may not be that many, but eventually, many more will realise the political games of Umno and PAS," he said.
de0b8307018769b1: SAN FRANCISCO: No startup has ever grown so fast. In five years, Anthropic has become an AI giant valued at US$1 trillion, and it is now aiming for a record-breaking stock market debut, even if its original ambitions have been watered down somewhat.
The San Francisco-based firm faces three threats: rivals that are catching up, prices that are collapsing, and bills that keep climbing.
Anthropic spelled out the risks in its Wall Street prospectus, the document that lays out its vision to potential investors.
The first is commoditisation: "the degree of differentiation among advanced AI models may narrow," the company warns.
Additionally, Anthropic says that "substantially all" of its revenue comes from its AI tools.
Unlike Google or Meta, it has no advertising empire to fall back on if business takes a hit, and no cloud business like Microsoft's.
Investors have already grown nervous.

In mid-August, shareholders were floating a valuation of US$2 trillion. However, quarter-on-quarter growth slowed from 145% in the second quarter to 45% in the third, cooling expectations to around US$1.3 trillion.
Cheap and open
So-called open AI models, which anyone can download and modify, are approaching the capabilities of closed models such as Claude or ChatGPT, which are available only through their owners' services.
Open models lag their closed counterparts by only about four months on average, according to research institute Epoch AI.
They include Kimi K3.1 Pro from Chinese company Moonshot, which costs half as much as Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic’s current flagship.
And among paid models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, none has stayed on top for long.
Anthropic also acknowledges it is holding itself back: its safety measures "could slow our capability gains relative to competitors that do not adopt similar constraints."
Still, the company says each new version of Claude has boosted sales. More than 80% of its revenue last quarter came from models less than six months old.
Prices collapsing

When products look alike, prices fall. According to Morningstar, the price of having AI process the same amount of text at the same level of performance has dropped 97%, from US$17 at the end of 2024 to 50 cents today.
Anthropic itself cut the price of Claude Opus by 20% in September, and OpenAI cut the price of one of its flagship models by a factor of five in July.
The effect is already visible at Vercel, a developer platform that routes requests across AI models.
In August, more than half of the text it handled was processed by open models, up from 13% in April.
Even so, Anthropic still captured nearly two-thirds of spending on the platform.
"Even a 90% price cut would not shrink total spending on AI as long as usage keeps growing at its current pace," said Malik Ahmed Khan, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar.
'Triple whammy'
Anthropic's costs, by contrast, are largely locked in. To stay ahead, each new Claude model has to be bigger than the last, trained on more data using more computing power.
Since late 2025, the company has committed to paying at least US$417 billion to rent chips and servers.
That is nearly 13 years of sales at its first-half 2026 pace, and the total could nearly double if cancelable or planned contracts are included.
These commitments are due no matter the state of its business, Anthropic warns.
The bet involves the entire industry: Google and Amazon are at once Anthropic's shareholders, its suppliers and its resellers.

If AI turns out to be less profitable than expected, the International Monetary Fund fears a "triple whammy" from these intertwined investments: falling stock prices, debts that are harder to repay, and promised revenue that never materializes.
The independent research firm New Constructs called the listing "an unprecedented test of investor gullibility."
To pay these bills, Anthropic is counting on money from the stock market, which is not unlimited.
SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket and AI company, raised record sums there in June, while Google and Meta, which are pouring fortunes into data centers, are also seeking fresh capital.
OpenAI, whose chief Sam Altman called a listing "ill-advised" this year, has chosen to wait until 2027, giving it time to see how Wall Street treats its big rival.

24664d28e9268f65: GUADALAJARA (Mexico), Nov 16 — Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the architect of modern Mexican drug trafficking known as “the boss of bosses,” who transformed the global cocaine trade and orchestrated the murder of a US agent, died yesterday at age 80, officials said.

The notorious drug kingpin, a former police officer who played a key role in forging alliances with Colombian traffickers, died in a hospital where he had been transferred from prison two days earlier.

“After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility” after “he suffered multiple organ failure,” according to a statement from the security ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.
Felix Gallardo’s health had deteriorated markedly in recent years, with conditions including high blood pressure, diabetes and deafness.

In 2022, then-president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador said he was “in very poor health.” A judge granted him house arrest, but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer.
One of the founders of the Guadalajara cartel, from which the Sinaloa cartel would later emerge, Felix Gallardo had been incarcerated since 1989 and was serving a 40-year sentence.
He was convicted for the 1985 murder of an undercover US Drug Enforcement Agency officer, Enrique “Kiki” Camarena Salazar, which outraged the United States.
Rise of the cartels
Felix Gallardo was a native of Sinaloa state, where he was born on January 8, 1946, according to public records.
His involvement in crime went virtually hand in hand with his career in the state and federal police.
He even served as a bodyguard to a Sinaloa governor, a role that experts say may have helped him secure the complicity and protection of powerful politicians.
He partnered with another veteran kingpin, Rafael Caro Quintero. Together with other crime bosses, they united gangs trafficking drugs to the United States and formed the Guadalajara cartel.
The cartel was formed around a “hegemonic model” and laid “the roots for nearly all of today’s drug trafficking activities,” according to InSight Crime, a website specialising in the drug trade.
Felix Gallardo “partnered with Colombian traffickers like Pablo Escobar, and became Escobar’s most important Mexico associate,” the publication said.
The Guadalajara gang controlled the country’s underworld, earning Felix Gallardo the nicknames El jefe de jefes and El Padrino — which translate to “the boss of bosses” and “the Godfather.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
File photo taken on January 1, 2005 of Felix Gallardo, member of the Guadalajara Cartel, at La Palma prison in Almoloya of Juarez, Mexico. — PGR/AFP pic
Downfall
Felix Gallardo was convicted for the February 1985 murder of Camarena Salazar, who was kidnapped and tortured.
The agent’s death remains an open wound for the United States.
Intense pressure from Washington led to the arrest in 1985 of Caro Quintero, who is now imprisoned in the United States on charges of drug trafficking and the agent’s murder.
Felix Gallardo was arrested in April 1989 but continued to control the criminal business from prison, according to experts.
He was serving his sentence at Puente Grande prison in Jalisco state.

The Guadalajara cartel imploded in the 1990s, and its local leaders formed regional cartels, including the Sinaloa cartel, built up by Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman and Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, both sentenced to life in prison in the United States.

Felix Gallardo remained in the popular imagination through narcocorridos, or drug ballads, such as El jefe de jefes, which is banned in public spaces, and Netflix dramas about drug trafficking, with Mexican actor Diego Luna portraying the kingpin. — AFP
e8988ed9da050a1f: KLANG, Nov 16 — Pakatan Harapan (PH) must focus its efforts on formulating a new political realignment as a strategy to form the government in the next general election, said PH election director Datuk Seri Amirudin Shari.

9c123a0f48cac67e: GENEVA: Major arms producers the US and Russia look set to oppose a push at a global meeting in Geneva this week to launch negotiations on legally binding rules for autonomous weapons, in what diplomats and rights groups expect to be difficult talks.
The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has boosted development of drones, robots, tanks, submarines and other military hardware capable of killing without human involvement.
Semi-autonomous, AI-assisted weapons have already been used in Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East, despite ethical concerns.
The UN-hosted meeting starting on Monday is due to decide whether to launch negotiations for a legally binding agreement on prohibitions and regulations for Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS).

However, while most of the 128 states party to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons support that, major military nations including the US, Russia and Israel oppose it, arguing that existing humanitarian law is sufficient.
The leaders of the UN and the International Committee of the Red Cross, along with the Pope, have all warned of the dangers from autonomous weapons and support regulation.

“Machines should never be allowed to decide who lives and dies on a battlefield but that is the dystopian reality that is fast approaching,” said Verity Coyle from Human Rights Watch, which is urging the Review Conference to take firm action.
Two diplomats told Reuters the discussions looked set to be challenging. But states could build bridges to find a compromise agreement by the end of the week, they said.
"All options are on the table, from legally binding to non-legally binding, as well as a hybrid agreement with both elements," one of the diplomats added.
Risk of error
Campaigners say autonomous weapons systems can behave unpredictably, raising the risk of fatal errors.

Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute – a US-based nonprofit organisation focused on reducing the risks of advanced technologies, including AI – said LAWS were no longer science fiction, pointing to media reporting of early use of fully autonomous systems in Ukraine.
The US favours guidelines over binding rules on LAWS, arguing that international law already provides a framework to govern warfare.
It has proposed a five-year mandate for talks towards a non-binding agreement.
The Red Cross says humanitarian law does not sufficiently address specific risks from autonomous weapons.
Russia has not publicly stated its position going into the talks, but has previously resisted proposals for a legally binding agreement.
It plans to block the EU, an observer to the talks, from taking the floor, a senior Western diplomat told Reuters.
Hehir told Reuters the US and Russia would probably seek to water down any outcome as they did in September with a text about autonomous weapons and their potential for harm.
The chair of this week's talks has proposed a two-year mandate to negotiate a legally binding protocol.
The UK, Germany and France propose negotiations on an instrument that leaves open whether it would be legally binding or not, Coyle told Reuters.
d196037a880de81b: JERUSALEM, Nov 16 — Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot yesterday said caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu “cannot remain at the head of the government for a minute longer”, following reports indicating alleged electoral interference by a Netanyahu aide.
A few hours after representatives of the two men met to discuss the possible formation of a national unity government, Eisenkot launched a scathing attack on his rival.
“The behaviour of the outgoing prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his entourage constitutes a concrete, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” said Eisenkot, a former army chief.

Israel’s Channel 12 had earlier reported that on the eve of the election, Netanyahu’s chief of staff Ido Norden had phoned in a complaint to the police commissioner’s office about members of the Arab-Israeli Raam party.
During this exchange, Norden reportedly directed police officers to a purported intelligence source who was a former employee of Netanyahu’s office, according to Channel 12.

Based on information from this source, three Raam members were arrested. Netanyahu subsequently launched an offensive against the Arab-Israeli parties, accusing them of electoral fraud after they gained a record number of seats.
The three men were later released when the police determined that the information provided by this source was unfounded.
“I call for the immediate opening of an investigation into this affair,” Eisenkot said yesterday, according to a statement from his party.
Netanyahu’s office responded by stating that Channel 12’s report was “false”, maintaining that Norden had “fulfilled his civic duty”.
Netanyahu’s Likud party accused Eisenkot of “outrageous incitement”.
“While the prime minister is extending a hand in the spirit of unity, Eisenkot and his associates issue daily statements filled with venomous, inflammatory attacks,” the party said in a statement.
The opposition has accused the caretaker premier of seeking to delegitimise Arab parties and the election in an attempt to cling to power.
Neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor Eisenkot’s opposition secured the 61 seats required to form a government following last month’s election.
The two main Arab parties, the Joint List and Raam, have indicated support for Eisenkot, who was tapped to form a government last week.
On Saturday, Netanyahu appealed to Eisenkot to join him in a unity government, but the former army chief accused him of playing “tricks” and sowing tensions. — AFP

d2ec6581b65c222b: International executives will gather in Kuala Lumpur on Nov 16-17 to discuss cruise opportunities in Malaysia and Southeast Asia. For Malaysia, this is a significant development.
It is the first time the event is being hosted here, reflecting the growing recognition of Malaysia's considerable potential to have a more important role in the regional cruise tourism industry.

The event, Seatrade Cruise Asia 2026, brings together more than 18 international cruise line brands, including some of the biggest names such as Royal Caribbean International, StarDream Cruises, Norwegian Cruise Line, MSC Cruises, Azamara, Disney Cruise Line and Princess Cruises.

Senior executives and industry representatives from Europe, the US and Asia will participate in discussions on the future of cruising in this region, including new itineraries, emerging destinations, home-porting opportunities, port infrastructure and the growing demand for cruise holidays among Asian travellers.

Indeed, the event is being organised across several Malaysian destinations, with Kuala Lumpur hosting the main conference, followed by activities in Penang and Langkawi. This provides an opportunity to showcase not just our ports but also the country's wider tourism attractions.
Malaysia's opportunity

For many years, Singapore has established itself as the principal cruise home port in Southeast Asia. Its strategic location, international airport connectivity, modern cruise terminals and well-developed tourism infrastructure have made it a natural starting point for many international cruise operators.
From Singapore, cruise itineraries frequently extend along the Straits of Malacca, with calls at Melaka, Port Klang, Penang and Langkawi before continuing towards Phuket in Thailand.

Another attractive itinerary, depending on the season and weather conditions, covers the eastern side of the peninsula, with destinations such as Tioman, Redang and neighbouring destinations including Koh Samui in Thailand. Further itineraries can extend towards Cambodia and Vietnam, which includes Sihanoukville, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang.

All these routes offer considerable opportunities for Malaysia. We have the geographical advantage of being located along some of the busiest and most established maritime tourism corridors in Southeast Asia.
We also have a diverse range of destinations, from historical cities and cultural attractions to islands, beaches, rainforests and natural landscapes.

However, geographical location alone does not guarantee success. Cruise operators are commercial businesses. They look at passenger demand, port accessibility, terminal facilities, operating costs, immigration procedures, shore excursions and the overall attractiveness of destinations before deciding where to deploy their vessels.
Growing Asian market
The timing is particularly important because the Asian cruise market is developing rapidly.

According to figures released by the Singapore Tourism Board, Southeast Asia recorded approximately 3.9 million cruise passenger visits in 2024. Singapore accounted for 48% of these visits, while Malaysia captured approximately 22%.
Together, the two countries accounted for around 70% of the growing regional market. These figures also demonstrate that Malaysia is already an important cruise destination.

However, it has also been suggested that there is considerable room to grow, particularly if we can attract more international cruise operators and encourage more Malaysians to experience cruise holidays.

The potential domestic market should not be underestimated either. Malaysia has a sizeable middle-income population, an expanding travelling public and a growing number of families looking for alternative holiday experiences.

Cruise holidays could become increasingly attractive, particularly for families who prefer an all-inclusive holiday package with accommodation, meals, entertainment and multiple destinations incorporated into one journey.
There is also an opportunity to develop more regional cruise packages catering specifically to Malaysian, Indonesian, Thai and other Southeast Asian travellers.
This is a growing market that cruise operators are looking to explore and I think Malaysia is ready for it.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

c392c4009025708f: PETALING JAYA: Menteri Besar Johor Onn Hafiz Ghazi membuat laporan polis dan aduan kepada Suruhanjaya Komunikasi dan Multimedia Malaysia (SKMM) berhubung penyebaran dakwaan tidak benar mengenai projek pembangunan dan kemudahan awam di negeri itu.

“Saya sentiasa terbuka menerima teguran, kritikan dan aduan daripada Bangsa Johor. Insya-Allah, setiap aduan akan disemak dan diambil tindakan.

Beliau berkata laporan polis dan aduan kepada SKMM dibuat supaya siasatan dapat dijalankan terhadap kesahihan akaun terbabit, kandungan yang disebarkan serta kemungkinan wujud aktiviti yang dilakukan secara berkoordinasi.

“Kita boleh berbeza pandangan, mengkritik dan tidak bersetuju, tetapi jangan sampai perbezaan politik dijadikan alasan untuk menyebarkan fitnah atau mengelirukan rakyat,” katanya.
Beliau turut menasihatkan rakyat Johor supaya lebih berhati-hati dengan maklumat yang tersebar di media sosial dan menyemak kesahihannya sebelum mempercayai atau menyebarkannya.
Onn Hafiz berharap siasatan pihak berkuasa dapat membawa kepada tindakan sewajarnya bagi melindungi keharmonian serta kemakmuran negeri itu daripada penyebaran fitnah dan maklumat tidak benar.
“Kepada seluruh Bangsa Johor, saya nasihatkan supaya sentiasa berhati-hati dan menyemak kesahihan setiap maklumat sebelum mempercayai atau menyebarkannya,” katanya.

3404d56f7837c1a0: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 16 — The Department of Environment (DOE) is conducting drone surveillance and deploying additional air quality monitoring equipment to investigate the significant difference in Air Pollutant Index (API) readings between the Batu Muda and Cheras stations here.

In a statement yesterday, the DOE said the measures were taken following API readings at the Batu Muda Air Quality Monitoring Station remaining at unhealthy levels of over 150 for the past two days, compared with the nearby Cheras station, which recorded readings of only around 60.

It said additional equipment had been installed near the Batu Muda station to obtain supporting data for technical analysis, with preliminary findings to be announced after 24 hours of monitoring and completion of the technical review.

“At the same time, drone-based air monitoring is also being conducted to help identify possible sources of air pollutant emissions, including open burning activities in the surrounding areas,” the statement said.
Earlier, the DOE said an investigation which began Nov 14 involved inspections of monitoring stations, field patrols and efforts to identify sources of pollution in the surrounding areas.
“Initial inspections found that the station was operating properly. However, further reviews are being conducted to verify the readings recorded.
“Patrols identified two small-scale open burning incidents, and both fires were extinguished on the same day,” the statement said.

The DOE reminded the public not to engage in open burning or allow their land and premises to be encroached upon by irresponsible parties, resulting in open burning, whether for specific purposes or accidentally.

Those convicted of an offence under Section 29(A) of the Environmental Quality Act 1974 may face a fine of up to RM1 million or imprisonment for up to five years, or both, in addition to a compound of up to 50 per cent of the maximum fine for each offence.
The public is also urged to help put out small fires and report open burning incidents to the Fire and Rescue Department at 999 or the DOE’s toll-free line at 1-800-88-2727.

The latest hourly API readings can be accessed via the website at https://eqms.doe.gov.my/APIMS/main or the official MyJAS EQMS application, which can be downloaded from Google Play or the App Store. — Bernama
e3efd4e4ac6c1b11: SINGAPORE: The yen was pinned near two-month lows against the dollar and little moved against the euro in early trade on Monday as markets assessed how an unexpected contraction in the Japanese economy in the third quarter affects the policy outlook.

The yen fluctuated between gains and losses without moving too far, trading against the dollar at 159.69 yen and against the euro t 176.04 yen, close to levels where US and Japanese authorities are believed to have intervened earlier this year.
"The stagnation in GDP in the third quarter probably won’t prevent the BOJ from tightening policy further at its upcoming meeting in December," Capital Economics said in a note.
"In fact, it looks increasingly likely that the Bank will have to tighten policy more aggressively than we’ve been anticipating as inflation is about to surge."
Asia's second-largest economy contracted by an annualised 0.1% in the July-September quarter, data showed, weaker than expectations of 0.3% growth.

Most other currency pairs held steady in early Asian trade. The euro last fetched US$1.1025, the British pound was level at US$1.3216, the Australian dollar was unchanged at US$0.6777 and its kiwi counterpart was steady at US$0.5523.

The dollar has been gaining strength against most of its peers after hawkish commentary from Federal Reserve officials and a hot October inflation report, which have revived bets that the US central bank will have to take aggressive action to rein in cost-of-living pressures.
The US dollar index, which measures the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, was trading at 103.44, its highest since April 2025.
The US central bank "has some work to do on inflation," said Kansas City Federal Reserve president Jeff Schmid on Sunday. He is not a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee this year.

Fed funds futures are pricing an implied 93.9% probability of a 25-basis-point hike at the US central bank's next two-day meeting ending on Dec 9, while assigning a 6% likelihood to a bigger 50-basis-point hike, down from 11.5% on Friday, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Traders have priced in four rate hikes by September next year, albeit by a slim margin, the tool shows.
The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was down 0.8 basis point at 5.143%.

In cryptocurrency markets, bitcoin edged up 0.2% to US$65,186.44, stabilising after a three-day rout that took the biggest digital asset to a four-month low during the weekend, while ether was up 0.7% at US$1,830.94.

54743034d7df7571: PETALING JAYA: Umno bigwigs eyeing a comeback in the next general election (GE16) risk throwing a spanner in the works of seat negotiations between Barisan Nasional (BN) and Perikatan Nasional (PN), say analysts.
Universiti Malaya's Tawfik Yaakub said Umno veteran Nazri Aziz's intention to contest in Padang Rengas again would trigger a conflict with PN, which currently holds the seat through Azahari Hasan.
Tawfik expects similar conflicts to surface over the seats of Gerik and Machang, which are held by Fathul Huzir Ayob and Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal of PN component Wawasan.

He said Gerik might be eyed by Umno secretary-general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki, who contested the seat in the 2022 general election (GE15), while Kelantan Umno chief Ahmad Jazlan Yaakub would be assessing his chances in Machang.
Asyraf lost the race in Gerik by 1,377 votes in GE15 while Jazlan was Machang MP for two terms before losing to Wan Fayhsal by 10,154 votes in the same general election.
Tawfik said this would be a key test for the BN-PN cooperation come GE16, particularly as the coalitions mull whether to stick to the principle of allowing incumbents to defend their seats.
"I see this issue as a true test of the sincerity of the BN-PN alliance.

"If they overly prioritise the interests of their leaders over candidate winnability, seat negotiations could become complicated and may even fail, resulting in clashes in several areas," he told FMT.
BN and PN started formally working together in the Aug 1 Negeri Sembilan election and continued their alliance in the recent Melaka polls, storming to two-thirds majorities in both.
With the Umno and PAS-led coalitions widely expected to continue their pact in GE16, PAS information chief Ahmad Fadhli Shaari has called for seat negotiations to commence earlier.
Mazlan Ali of Universiti Teknologi Malaysia believes Wawasan will not be willing to make way for BN in seats that its MPs, or those linked to the party, won in GE15.

This is despite the party making way for BN in Sungai Udang during the Melaka polls, although its now former assemblyman Dr Aleef Yusof won the seat in the 2021 polls. Aleef was with Bersatu at the time.
Mazlan said PAS's intention to defend every seat it won in GE15 added further complexities, given that the Islamic party wiped out Umno in Perlis, Kedah, Kelantan and Terengganu.
"This will make it hard for Umno to demand its traditional strongholds," he said.
He said this called for compromise and a focus on prioritising candidates with greater winnability.
"Failure to manage these internal rivalries could affect the pact between both coalitions and benefit Pakatan Harapan," he added.

c6255a3cd633e727: KUALA LUMPUR: Just a few years ago, teenager Mung Pi was struggling to grasp basic mathematical concepts, having missed out on years of formal education.

Financial difficulties and documentation issues made his education a constant uncertainty. His family could barely afford his examination fees, and there were times when he was unsure if he could attend school the following month.

Today, however, Mung Pi has defied the odds, achieving straight A*s in his 2025 International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE) examinations. He also earned a perfect score in English as a Second Language, securing the prestigious Top in the World award.
It is a remarkable transformation for someone who once faced seemingly insurmountable obstacles in his pursuit of an education.
“I feel incredibly proud and honoured, but most of all, pleasantly surprised. I honestly didn’t expect to achieve the results that I received,” Mung Pi, 19, told FMT Lifestyle.
“I am truly grateful and feel a sense of accomplishment. I couldn’t have done it without the continuous support from teachers, friends, and family.”
Originally from Myanmar, Mung Pi was just three when he arrived in the country with his parents and older brother.
A lack of funds, however, meant his education was frequently disrupted. He moved between learning centres, sometimes staying home when his family could not afford the fees.

Things worsened when his father fell seriously ill and could no longer work, leaving his mother as the sole breadwinner. His brother eventually had to leave school to find a job, sacrificing his own education so Mung Pi could continue his.
In 2024, Mung Pi was offered a place at Dignity for Children Foundation, an organisation offering education and support to underprivileged children.
But even with this opportunity, he faced an uphill battle. With the IGCSE exams approaching, Mung Pi had to catch up on years of missed education in a relatively short time.

Initially, he spent countless nights reading and writing, believing that studying for hours was the only way to overcome his academic shortcomings. Eventually, however, he realised that a different approach was needed.
“I took the time to fully reflect on my strengths and weaknesses, learning habits, and the subjects I was studying,” he explained.
He began developing personalised study plans for each subject, making learning more manageable, rewarding and, most importantly, enjoyable.
Nevertheless, there were setbacks. After narrowly failing a chemistry test, Mung Pi began questioning whether he was even capable of succeeding.
“But I remembered my brother, who was working to put food on our table while I sat in a classroom. I thought, what might he have become if given the same chance?
"I knew his sacrifice could not be for nothing."

Financial difficulties also remained a major concern. Luckily, welfare assistance and a Dignity sponsorship programme provided support, helping Mung Pi achieve results that exceeded even his own expectations.

Today, he is a teacher with the foundation, hoping to provide other children with the same opportunities he received. He has secured a scholarship to pursue his A-levels at UCSI University next year, and hopes to eventually become an IGCSE teacher.
For students facing similar challenges, Mung Pi’s advice is to understand their learning habits, practise regularly, and always ask questions.

“Being able to achieve such results is truly something to be grateful for, proud of, and aim for, but the journey isn’t always so enjoyable. So my last but personal favourite bit of advice is to make it fun.
“Explore different ways to write down notes. Reward yourself at the end of your study time. Study at a friend’s house, put stickers on your books. Whatever makes it fun for you.”
2288d9f6131aeac1: SAN PEDRO SULA: A new caravan of more than 100 migrants set off on foot from Honduras towards the US on Sunday, an AFP journalist observed.
The group was seen carrying backpacks and water for the long journey, despite warnings from US president Donald Trump to stay away.

The migrants, some carrying children in their arms, left the bus terminal in San Pedro Sula, in the north of the Central American country, shortly before 4pm. They aim to reach Corinto, on the border with Guatemala.
"We're going with the intention of working," Alexander Vallecillo, an 18-year-old bricklayer who is leaving his wife and eight-month-old son behind in Honduras, told AFP.
"With the situation here, you can't get ahead," Vallecillo lamented.
The caravan's final destination is the US, even as Trump, who lost control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov 3 midterm elections, maintains a crackdown on irregular migration.
Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Mexico if it fails to stop the migrants.
The US embassy in Tegucigalpa has also warned that caravans that "cross illegally" will face legal consequences.
"The laws did not change after the Nov 3 elections," it posted on X.
"That man [Trump] is a bad person. We hope the results [of the congressional elections] will help us a little," Vallecillo said.
Another caravan of around 1,000 Central Americans reached Mexico in early November, while a separate group of around 100 migrants was dispersed by Mexican authorities this month.
On Friday, following Trump's tariff threat, president Claudia Sheinbaum said there were "no more caravans" of migrants travelling through Mexico toward its northern neighbour.
According to Sheinbaum, Mexico has broken up 24 caravans since Trump's return to power in 2024.
Estela Rodriguez, the mother of two girls, aged two and five, said she decided to migrate after a criminal organisation tried to extort money from her cake business.
The situation in the US "is complicated," but "it's worse here, and you have a family to support," Rodriguez, a 20-year-old businesswoman who is also travelling alone, told AFP.

bf312d23834f27d5: JAKARTA: Indonesian authorities may struggle to put a floor under Asia’s worst-performing currency, according to strategists, as rising domestic political uncertainty and further capital outflows weigh on the rupiah.

BNP Paribas SA expects the rupiah to plummet to 18,500 per dollar by the end of next year, while MUFG Bank sees it weakening to 18,350 this quarter. Mizuho Bank also expects further downside for the Indonesian currency, which dropped to an all-time low against the dollar last week.

Investors have soured on Indonesian assets this year on concerns over President Prabowo Subianto’s economic policy direction, the ouster of key economic policymakers and MSCI’s threat of a double downgrade of the country’s equity market.

Adding to the bearish sentiment were the resignation last week of Prabowo’s deputy, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, and growing bets on Federal Reserve rate hikes that have pushed the dollar to an 18-month high.

“Investors will probably maintain their conservatism toward these risks by demanding premium for potential negative catalysts on the horizon, and the rupiah will face pressures as a result,” said Homin Lee, senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier in Singapore.
The rupiah has slumped about 9% so far this year, putting it on track for its worst annual performance since 2022. It closed at 18,195 per dollar on Friday.

Bank Indonesia has used an array of tools to stabilise the rupiah, but with limited success. It regularly intervenes in the currency’s spot market as well as offshore and onshore non-deliverable forwards. The central bank has also been buying government bonds in the secondary market to stem a selloff partly triggered by higher Treasury yields and elevated oil prices.

Still, foreign funds have sold a net US$5.6 billion of Indonesian stocks this year as the MSCI warning drove the benchmark index to its lowest level in six years. A further US$5.6 billion in passive outflows is possible if the country’s stocks are removed from MSCI’s indexes, Goldman Sachs Group Inc. estimates.

Now, dwindling net foreign reserves may also limit the central bank’s ability to continue intervening in the market, said Parisha Saimbi, a currency and rates strategist at BNP Paribas. The French bank sees a risk of the rupiah reaching its target earlier, she said.

A slim majority of analysts in a Bloomberg survey expect Bank Indonesia to once again keep borrowing costs unchanged when it meets on Wednesday. It left the benchmark rate unchanged in October while unveiling hedging incentives aimed at attracting foreign inflows and supporting the rupiah.

“A 25-basis-point rate hike on Nov 18 is probably not going to be enough now as markets want to see a central bank that is using basic monetary policy tools to the full extent, rather than relying on backstage measures,” said Simon Quijano-Evans, head of strategy at Macro Hive.
Still, a sustained decline in oil prices on the back of easing Middle East tensions could support the rupiah given Indonesia’s reliance on energy imports.
“We think the resolution of Iran-related risks can go a long way in stabilizing investor sentiment at some point, but the pressures on the rupiah will remain in the near-term,” Lombard’s Lee said.
4825a6258fc6da6f: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 16 — The proposed Nutrition Bill, illegal cryptocurrency mining and the expansion of electric vehicle (EV) charging station infrastructure are among the issues to be discussed in the Dewan Rakyat today.

According to the Order Paper published on Parliament’s official website, Rodziah Ismail (PH-Ampang) will ask the Health Minister during the oral question-and-answer session about the timeline for drafting the proposed Bill to regulate the nutritional intake of the public.

She also wants details on the Bill’s objectives, main scope, overall cost and mechanisms to ensure the participation of health experts, industry players, non-governmental organisations, the public and other stakeholders in its drafting and implementation.

In the same session, Datuk Ngeh Koo Ham (PH-Beruas) will ask the Home Minister why illegal cryptocurrency mining activities are rampant in Manjung, Perak, and why those involved are difficult to apprehend and bring to justice.

Meanwhile, Datuk Seri Hishammuddin Tun Hussein (BN-Sembrong) will ask the Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry about the ministry’s plans to expand EV charging station infrastructure to rural areas and small towns to encourage the adoption of green technology.

Also listed is a question from Mohamad Shafizan Kepli (GPS-Batang Lupar) to the Transport Minister on measures to improve safety management and emergency response at all short take-off and landing airports (STOLports) operating in Sarawak, following the helicopter crash in Long Lellang on Sept 8.

The Dewan Rakyat sitting will then proceed with the tabling of the Finance Bill 2026 and the Measures for the Collection, Administration and Enforcement of Tax Bill 2026 by the Finance Minister for first reading.
After that, the sitting will resume the committee-stage debate on the Supply (Budget 2027) Bill, followed by scheduled replies from the Works Ministry and the Transport Ministry.
According to the Dewan Rakyat calendar, the committee-stage debate on Budget 2027 will continue until Nov 26, with 16 more ministries scheduled to conclude their respective winding-up sessions.
The Third Meeting of the Fifth Session of the 15th Parliament currently runs for 37 days until Dec 8. — Bernama

92fe9397d7bd8d24: KUALA LUMPUR: With practised fingers, Buniamin Abdullah loops and knots a nylon line around a simple gauge, steadily building one mesh after another.
At 73, his eyesight may no longer be what it was, but the skill he inherited from his parents remains firmly in his hands.

Affectionately known as Abah, the Pasir Mas native, who now lives in Kota Bharu, has been making traditional fishing nets since 1987 - almost four decades spent repeating a craft that requires little machinery but a great deal of patience.

Although he no longer has the strength to venture out onto the open sea, Buniamin told Bernama that net-making has taken on another purpose in his later years: it gives him something absorbing and calming to do.
“Whenever I feel bored, I turn to this work. It puts my mind at ease because my attention is focused solely on making the net meshes,” he said during a demonstration at the National Museum recently.

The tools of his trade are modest. A "belira", or measuring gauge, determines the size of each opening, while a specialised netting needle known as a "chobe" carries the nylon line used to weave and knot the net.

But simple tools do not make for simple work. Each knot must be repeated thousands of times, with the belira ensuring the openings remain uniform. Prawn nets typically have finer meshes of about 1.9cm, while those intended for fish measure more than 2.5cm.
“For finer nets, you need a finer needle. For larger nets, you use a bigger needle,” Buniamin explained.

The size of the mesh affects not only the needle he uses but also the level of concentration required. Neatness and consistency matter throughout, since even small variations become increasingly obvious across an entire net.
A smaller net measuring around 274cm can take him about 20 days to complete. Larger ones require more than a month, depending on the size and fineness of the mesh.
That amount of work is reflected in the price. Buniamin’s handmade nets remain in demand and start at around RM500 each, with the final cost depending on their size and complexity.
Increasingly, however, age is setting its own limits: Buniamin said deteriorating eyesight has made it harder for him to produce nets with particularly fine meshes.
For a man who learnt the skill from his own parents, there is some reassurance in knowing the thread has not stopped with him.
The father of three, grandfather of 13 and great-grandfather of nine has taught the craft to a son and daughter as well as several of his grandchildren.
“If we want this craft to survive, we must teach our children so they can carry on the work," he noted.
It is a small but significant continuation at a time when handmade fishing gear increasingly has to compete with cheaper, mass-produced alternatives.

Kelantan Museum Corporation senior assistant curator Shahrul Hisham Abdul Ra-aid said machine-made nets cost considerably less because they can be produced in bulk, while their handmade counterparts demand far more time and labour.

“There are still people who are skilled in making handmade nets, but their numbers are small,” he said. “Most of those who still make traditional fishing nets and fish traps are from the older generation, while interest among young people is declining.”

That is precisely why craftspeople such as Buniamin were invited to demonstrate their skills at the national museum. “We want the public to witness firsthand how fishing nets are made by hand, rather than simply viewing the finished products,” Shahrul added.
a8becbed55c716fd: On Saturday, Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Ismail Lasim confirmed he had withdrawn a letter sent to the Keeper of the Rulers’ Seal concerning the “removal” of Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan.
The letter was also understood to affirm the unanimous support of the 10 sacked executive council members for Tuanku Muhriz.

This brings us to the million-ringgit question: can we trust Negeri Sembilan Umno? Is there any sincerity in what they say? Or is this yet another sleight of hand in an attempt to topple the state ruler?
Tuanku Muhriz's recent public rebuke of Ismail does not paint the latter as someone trustworthy.
There are four reasons why I remain wary of Ismail’s actions.

1. Why is Ismail retracting the letter only now? My theory is that he needs the ruler’s consent to convene the state assembly. While one could, on paper, administer a state without executive councillors, a state assembly sitting is needed to pass budgets and proposed laws.
Which raises this question: is Ismail really remorseful for his actions? Or is he acting out of desperation?
2. Ismail’s actions amid the controversy

They speak volumes about the man himself. He previously said he was coerced into signing a document deposing Tuanku Muhriz, only to later endorse a state executive council statement announcing the ruler’s purported removal.
On Aug 2, Ismail took his oath of office as menteri besar and pledged allegiance to Tuanku Muhriz before signing a proclamation the following day to remove the ruler.
There is a saying, “once bitten, twice shy”. In this instance though, we should be shy four times over.
3. There is still the matter of the other undangs (traditional territorial chieftains), some of whom have been removed, and the matter of the person whom they appointed as the state’s new ruler.

This faction, which is still alive and kicking, has apparently shown no remorse for its actions by openly challenging a Dewan Keadilan dan Undang Negeri Sembilan gazette notice formalising the removal of two chieftains and a customary leader.
It is said that this faction is close to Umno assemblymen in Negeri Sembilan. Mind you, none of the Umno assemblymen have come out to publicly distance themselves from this faction.
So how can we, the people, have any faith in Ismail’s retraction of a letter when Umno is presumably still linked to the said faction?

4. Has Ismail provided assurance via a written and signed declaration that he and his band of Umno men will never again conspire with others to overthrow Tuanku Muhriz? If Ismail were truly repentant, he would have gone the extra mile to show it.

Now, Umno’s decisive win at the Melaka polls will give the party some bragging rights following the controversies over former prime minister Najib Razak’s house arrest and the finances of Felda or Tabung Haji, which did not dent support for the party.
A resurgent Umno is likely to be emboldened to pull off another stunt in Negeri Sembilan, seeing as how the first one didn’t pan out exactly as they planned.
Ismail Lasim and Negeri Sembilan Umno give me very little reason to trust this mea culpa.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
5a2587b6eab93678: Sabtu lalu, Menteri Besar Negeri Sembilan, Ismail Lasim, mengesahkan beliau telah menarik balik surat yang dihantar kepada Penyimpan Mohor Besar Raja-Raja berhubung 'penyingkiran' Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan.

Ada pepatah yang berbunyi, 'sekali terkena, dua kali beringat'. Namun, dalam keadaan ini, kita sepatutnya empat kali beringat.
3. Isu Undang Luak yang masih belum selesai
Masih terdapat isu membabitkan Undang Luak, termasuk beberapa orang yang telah diturunkan, serta individu yang dilantik oleh mereka sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar yang baharu.

Kumpulan ini masih rancak dengan aktiviti mereka, dilihat tidak menunjukkan sebarang kekesalan atas tindakan mereka apabila secara terbuka mencabar notis warta Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU) yang mengesahkan penyingkiran dua Undang dan seorang pemimpin adat.
Dikatakan kumpulan ini mempunyai hubungan rapat dengan Adun Umno Negeri Sembilan. Perlu diingat, tiada seorang pun Adun Umno tampil secara terbuka menolak kumpulan tersebut.
Jadi, bagaimana kita sebagai rakyat boleh menaruh kepercayaan terhadap tindakan Ismail menarik balik surat itu sedangkan Umno dipercayai masih mempunyai kaitan dengan kumpulan berkenaan?

4. Adakah Ismail memberikan jaminan melalui perisytiharan bertulis yang ditandatangani bahawa beliau dan kumpulan anggota Umnonya tidak akan sekali-kali lagi berpakat dengan pihak lain untuk menjatuhkan Tuanku Muhriz? Jika Ismail benar-benar insaf, beliau sepatutnya menunjukkan lebih untuk membuktikannya.

Kini, kemenangan besar Umno dalam PRN Melaka akan memberikan parti itu sedikit kelebihan untuk berbangga susulan kontroversi isu tahanan rumah bekas perdana menteri Najib Razak serta kewangan Felda dan Tabung Haji, yang tidak menjejaskan sokongan terhadap parti itu.
Umno yang kembali bangkit berkemungkinan akan lebih berani untuk melakukan satu lagi tindakan serupa di Negeri Sembilan, memandangkan percubaan pertama mereka tidak berjalan seperti yang dirancang.
Tak banyak sebab untuk saya mempercayai Ismail dan Umno Negeri Sembilan ini benar-benar insaf dengan kesalahan mereka.

0764d7f910b686c5: TOKYO: Japan's economy contracted by an annualised 0.1% in the July-September quarter, government data showed on Monday, reflecting weak consumer spending as households grappled with elevated living costs.
The first contraction in four quarters underscores the uneven nature of Japan's economic recovery, with households remaining vulnerable to persistent inflation despite rising wages.

Still, the weakness is unlikely to be viewed by policymakers as a brake on Japan's moderate recovery, with resilient corporate activity, rising real wages and robust demand for artificial intelligence-related investment underpinning growth.
The gross domestic product data compared with a median market forecast of 0.3% annualised growth in a Reuters poll, and followed a revised 1.7% expansion in the previous quarter.
The reading translated into a quarterly fallof 0.02%, compared with the median estimate of a 0.1% increase.
Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of economic output, fell 0.3%, compared with a market estimate of a 0.2% decline.

Household spending was hurt by persistent price pressures and poor weather, including heavy rain and typhoons during the quarter. Demand for automobiles and air conditioners retreated following the temporary boost in the previous quarter from tax and regulatory changes.
Capital spending, a key driver of private demand, rose 1.6%, versus a market forecast for a 1.5% increase, backed by investment in labour-saving technologies and AI-related projects.
Net external demand, or exports minus imports, knocked 0.6 percentage point off growth, compared with a market forecast for a 0.4 percentage point drag on GDP growth.
Imports rose sharply as oil and other energy purchases recovered after Japan diversified procurement following disruptions linked to the war in the Middle East.
The latest data will be closely scrutinised by the Bank of Japan as it assesses whether the economy can withstand further interest-rate increases.

With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ has stepped up its policy tightening this year, delivering interest rate hikes in June and September.

A monthly survey by the Japan Center for Economic Research of 37 economists showed Japan's economy is expected to grow 0.89% in fiscal 2026 and 1.02% in fiscal 2027, suggesting economists see growth remaining modest but resilient.

Japan's longer-term growth challenges remain in focus, with the International Monetary Fund projecting the country will slip to the world's sixth-largest economy in nominal dollar terms in 2027 in dollar terms, overtaken by India and Britain. Japan is currently the world's fourth-largest after Germany.

13c955d113761972: It began, as most modern Malaysian sagas do, not with a bang, but with a grumble. A mamak shop, that near-sacred 24-hour temple of roti canai and teh tarik, had the audacity to close its doors on Deepavali day.

The reason? To allow its staff, many of whom are Hindus, to celebrate the Festival of Lights. A simple, humane and frankly logical decision. And yet, within hours, it had ignited a firestorm on social media, transforming a shop’s holiday schedule into a national debate on race, religion and the soul of our nation.
This can only happen in Malaysia. “Mamak tutup? On Deepavali? How can a Muslim-run restaurant close for a Hindu-based celebration?” So began the stream of religious insults and slurs.

For most people, the mamak shop is more than a restaurant; it is a cultural institution, a neutral ground where everyone can sit side-by-side at 3am, arguing over football or who should be the prime minister.

But the debate triggered by the post made out the closure to be almost a betrayal of the social contract. The real fireworks began when the keyboard warriors logged on and the debate fractured along predictable, yet deeply depressing, lines.

On one side, some who described the closure as an act of placing Deepavali celebrations over Islam, an analogy that is mind-boggling. On the other side, those who celebrated the closure as a victory for inclusivity, while simultaneously weaponising it against the owners. A simple act of employee appreciation became a truncheon in the never-ending racial culture war.

The comments sections devolved into a cesspool of racial slurs and religious mockery. The practices of each community – from fasting to praying to celebrating – were dissected, mocked and used as ammunition.

This is the Malaysian paradox. We are a nation that prides itself on our diversity, our muhibbah spirit and our ability to live together. We celebrate each other's festivals with open houses and open hearts. But the moment a minor racial or religious issue is raised, the harmony ruptures and the nation's ugly, tribalistic underbelly is exposed for all to see.

The debate exposed a deep-seated insecurity, the fear of being marginalised, anxiety over the “other” and the constant, exhausting need to assert one's own identity in a multi-racial landscape. The mamak shop became a proxy for a much larger, unresolved national conversation about what it means to be Malaysian.

The fact that we lose our minds over such a small matter is precisely the problem. We have become experts at finding offence, at drawing battle lines over the most trivial of issues. A shop closure becomes a religious war. A wrong word becomes a racial slur. A difference in opinion becomes a declaration of enmity.
We are so quick to insult each other, yet so slow to extend the basic courtesy of understanding.

The next time you see a shop closed for a holiday that isn't “yours”, take a breath. Instead of reaching for your phone to type a scathing comment, maybe reach for a packet of murukku from a Hindu neighbour.
The mamak shop will reopen, but the damage done by our own intolerance, the scars we inflict on our national psyche with every hateful comment, are far harder to heal.
Only in Malaysia can a day of light be turned into a war of darkness. Sadly, that is the most Malaysian thing of all.

5e7523689d328c72: PETALING JAYA: Dating may be about chemistry, companionship and getting to know someone better. But there is another element increasingly difficult to ignore - the bill.

A recent report found that 49.3% of Malaysian respondents considered dating expensive, while just 13.2% described it as cheap. More than half (52.6%) said they typically spent between RM51 and RM200 each time they went out.

Food and drinks dominated the budget, cited by 92.8% of respondents, while malls and cafés or restaurants were overwhelmingly the most common places for dates. Gifts, transport and entertainment such as arcade games and cinema tickets added further to the cost.
Yet the financial burden did not appear to fall evenly. Among male respondents, 59.3% said they usually covered the entire bill, while only 8.2% of women said the same.
Women were much more likely to say couples took turns paying, at 50.8%, or that their partner usually paid, at 32.8%.
That difference appears to be reflected in how the sexes experience the cost of dating. Some 27.5% of men said dating put them under financial pressure, compared with 16.4% of women.
More strikingly, 13.2% of men said they had gone into debt specifically to pay for dating, compared with 4.9% of women.
First dates appear to bring their own spending expectations. Nearly six in 10 men, or 59.3%, said they were willing to spend more on a first date, compared with 23% of women.

And once a relationship is established, spending does not necessarily ease off: 76.3% of all respondents said they would be willing to spend more to maintain a relationship, including 79.1% of men and 72.1% of women.

At the same time, most respondents seemed to have a fairly clear idea of what constitutes a reasonable date. Nearly three-quarters (74.4%) placed the ideal cost between RM50 and RM200, broadly matching what many said they already spent.

The findings, however, come with an important limitation. The survey, conducted from May 20 to June 13, involved just 152 respondents and explicitly states that its results should not be taken as representative of Malaysia as a whole.
The sample also skewed young: 43.4% were aged 18 to 24, while more than half lived in Selangor or Kuala Lumpur.

Still, the results offer an interesting glimpse into the economics of modern dating. Romance may not come with a fixed price tag but, for some Malaysians and particularly men, keeping up with the cost of going out appears to be creating very real financial pressure.
