90f0751c0696ac91: Microsoft has announced massive price rises for commercial cloud services in India and New Zealand, but a substantial reduction in China.
The software giant sells its cloudy services in many local currencies, at an equivalent rate to the prices it charges in the USA.
As exchange rates shift, so do the prices Microsoft charges around the world.

Microsoft last week announced the new charges that will come into effect from January 1, 2027, and the news isn’t pleasant for customers in India, who face an increase of 15.7 percent for cloud services and up to 20 percent for some on-prem offerings. New Zealand customers face a ten percent price hike.
Customers in China, where Microsoft relies on a local partner called 21Vianet to deliver its cloud, will see costs fall by up to 8.5 percent.
Australian buyers will see costs fall by 4.5 percent. The only nation not in Asia on Microsoft’s list is Norway, where prices will ease 5.9 percent.
Sega Japan hits double trouble
Sega has just had a rotten week that saw it battle a data leak and an outage.

The outage impacted the company’s ALL.Net and Aime services, which connect arcade games across different locations. The services include administrative features for arcade operators, plus services for gamers including pre-payment to play, high score and profile recording, and networked gaming.
Sega suspended some ALL.Net and Aime services on November 1 after discovering unauthorized access to servers. At least thirteen games and services were then unavailable until around November 15.
The company hasn’t explained what went wrong, but assured customers the incident was not a data breach and that payment information was safe.

But data did leak for those who subscribe to some Sega newsletters. Sega uses a third-party outfit called Arara Co. to send some emails, and it leaked email addresses. No other personal data leaked from Arara. Sega has nonetheless warned newsletter recipients to watch out for suspicious messages.
Alibaba floats chip unit
Chinese tech giant Alibaba last week announced its intention to float its T-Head chip design biz on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

The filing announcing the spinoff describes T-Head as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China,” suggesting Alibaba doesn’t think buyers in the rest of the world are keen to acquire its chips.

T-Head going public “allows a more efficient deployment of Alibaba Group’s financial resources,” the filing states, and should also mean the chip design outfit can more easily find third-party customers.
India bans export of dead batteries
The government of India last week banned the export of “Lithium-Ion battery Black Mass” – a powdery substance created during the process of recycling batteries.

“It contains recoverable quantities of critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese,” according to the government’s announcement of the ban, which argues the measure “will increase domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, thereby reducing import dependence and the associated foreign exchange outgo. It will also strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage and clean-energy technologies.”

“Further, the measure will advance the circular economy and ‘urban mining’, reducing reliance on primary mining, while supporting environmentally sound recycling of this hazardous material within the country in accordance with applicable environmental regulations.”
Japanese giants to investigate orbiting datacenters

Five giant Japanese companies – NTT, Mitsubishi Electric, MUFG Bank, the Development Bank of Japan, and telco NTT DOCOMO – last week signed a memorandum of understanding that will see them jointly explore development and operation of a mega-constellation of satellites.

The five “will examine the technical and business feasibility of commercializing a diverse range of services enabled by mega-constellations, including communications, Earth observation, satellite-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), and space data centers.”

Mitsubishi already works with the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to jointly develop and manufacture rockets. The two banks regularly back big infrastructure projects, while the two NTT entities have advanced comms expertise.
The five companies didn’t set a deadline for delivery of a plan.

If they do decide there’s a business opportunity, they’ll likely need to look beyond Japan for launch capacity as JAXA does not currently possess a re-usable launch vehicle and operates at a modest launch cadence compared to private launch operators. ®

More than 7,500 signatories identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company's workforce.
The support illustrates the unique standing of the leather-jacketed executive, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry.
Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing data centres and startups, earning it the nickname "the central bank of AI."
But the company has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble.
Huang championed open AI models, including Chinese ones, and fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.
According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return with people close to him, and one of his allies says he is assembling a crisis team of executives to seek White House support.

"They need a dramatic shake-up," Bessent said on Fox News, demanding that the company explain whether it had knowingly turned a blind eye to the smuggling of its chips to China.

ca3fb6a2f4f09231: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 16 — You see it every month on your payslip: a small deduction labelled Socso, amounting to just a few ringgit.
For some, they know that it is another statutory deduction made alongside their Employees Provident Fund (EPF) contributions and income tax.
But not many know exactly what that money pays for.

Unlike EPF, which primarily helps Malaysians build retirement savings, the Social Security Organisation (Socso) or Perkeso (Pertubuhan Keselamatan Sosial) as it is sometimes referred to, provides protection against employment-related accidents, occupational diseases, permanent disability and certain other circumstances, depending on the scheme and eligibility requirements.
With Budget 2027 introducing new incentives to expand social protection among gig workers and the self-employed, you may want to pay attention to some of these changes.
Here is how Socso works, what is new and what to look out for.
What is Socso?
Socso is essentially designed to provide financial assistance, medical care and rehabilitation to eligible workers when circumstances affect their ability to earn a living.
For employees in the private sector, contributions are generally shared between employers and employees.

Under the standard First Category contribution scheme, which generally covers employees below 60 years old, employers contribute 1.75 per cent of an employee’s monthly wages while employees contribute 0.5 per cent, according to the prescribed contribution schedule.
This means the contribution is not borne entirely by workers, with employers paying the larger share.
The money goes towards financing social protection benefits rather than being accumulated in an individual savings account like EPF.
Socso administers several protection schemes, including the Employment Injury Scheme, Invalidity Scheme and the newer Non-Employment Injury Scheme, known as Lindung 24 Jam.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Socso administers several protection schemes, including the Employment Injury Scheme, Invalidity Scheme and the newer Non-Employment Injury Scheme, known as Lindung 24 Jam. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
How does Socso work?
One of Socso’s main functions is to protect employees against accidents that happen while carrying out their jobs.
However, its protection is not limited to accidents inside the workplace.

Under the Employment Injury Scheme, workers may also receive protection for commuting accidents, including those occurring while travelling between their homes and workplaces, provided they follow the route without an unauthorised interruption or deviation.
This means a worker who gets involved in an accident while travelling to work may qualify for Socso benefits, subject to the scheme’s conditions.
The protection also covers accidents during work-related journeys and certain emergencies at the workplace, as well as occupational diseases arising from employment.
Depending on the circumstances, eligible workers can receive several forms of assistance:
Medical benefits: Medical treatment at Socso panel clinics or government hospitals for employment-related injuries or occupational diseases, subject to the applicable conditions.
Temporary disablement benefit: Financial assistance when an employee is temporarily unable to work because of an employment injury.
The daily rate is generally 80 per cent of the employee’s average assumed daily wage, subject to prescribed minimum and maximum limits.

To qualify, the employee must be on medical leave certified by a doctor for at least four days, including the day of the accident. The benefit is not payable for days when the employee works and receives wages.

Permanent disablement benefit: Financial assistance for workers who suffer permanent disabilities resulting from employment injuries. The daily rate is generally 90 per cent of the average assumed daily wage, subject to prescribed minimum and maximum limits and medical assessment.
Rehabilitation: Physical and vocational rehabilitation, including physiotherapy, occupational therapy, prosthetics and skills training to help injured workers return to employment where possible.
Dependents’ benefit: Financial assistance for eligible family members if an insured employee dies as a result of an employment injury.
Funeral benefit: Financial assistance of up to RM3,000 for eligible cases, subject to the actual funeral expenses incurred.
Socso is not simply about reimbursing medical expenses as it also provides a measure of income protection when an accident prevents someone from returning to work.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Socso is not simply about reimbursing medical expenses as it also provides a measure of income protection when an accident prevents someone from returning to work. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
Does Socso cover a person who becomes seriously ill outside of work?
Yes, it does but under a separate scheme.
The Invalidity Scheme provides 24-hour protection to eligible employees who suffer from a permanent medical condition, whether or not it is related to their employment.

To qualify, the condition must be certified by the Medical Board or Appellate Medical Board and leave the employee unable to earn at least one-third of the customary earnings of a healthy person with comparable abilities. Employees must also meet the scheme’s contribution requirements.
For example, an employee who develops a serious medical condition outside working hours that permanently affects their ability to earn a living may qualify for assistance.
Benefits include:
Invalidity pension: A monthly pension for eligible employees who have been medically certified as suffering from invalidity and meet the contribution requirements.
Invalidity grant: A lump-sum payment for eligible insured individuals who do not qualify for the monthly pension but meet the relevant contribution conditions.
Survivors’ pension: Financial assistance for eligible dependents if an insured person dies, subject to the scheme’s conditions.
Rehabilitation: Access to certain physical rehabilitation facilities and medical assistance, including dialysis.

Note that, while the Employment Injury Scheme covers accidents and occupational diseases arising from employment, the Invalidity Scheme provides protection against qualifying invalidity regardless of whether the condition is work-related.
In other words, Socso’s protection is not confined to accidents at the office or factory.
Can Socso protect you against accidents outside of working hours?
Yes. This is where the newer Non-Employment Injury Scheme, known as Lindung 24 Jam, comes in.
Introduced on June 1, 2026, the scheme extends protection to eligible employees who suffer accidental injuries outside working hours that are unrelated to their employment.
For example, an employee who is injured while carrying out personal activities during the weekend may qualify for protection under this scheme.
The benefits include medical treatment and other disablement benefits, subject to the scheme’s eligibility requirements.
However, Lindung 24 Jam does not cover every illness or accident.
Among its exclusions are:
Injuries caused by illnesses such as diabetes, fever and high blood pressure.
Accidents occurring outside Malaysia.
Injuries arising from self-employment, which fall under a separate social security scheme.
Domestic injuries covered under the Housewives’ Social Security Scheme.
Socso’s current guidance states that participation is voluntary for local employees, while it remains mandatory for foreign workers. Contributions are fully borne by employees who participate.
For local employees, this means the Lindung 24 Jam contribution is separate from the standard employment injury and invalidity contributions.
The contribution rate is being introduced in phases:
0.75 per cent for the first two years.
1 per cent for the following three years.
1.25 per cent from the sixth year onwards.
Employers are responsible for deducting and remitting the contribution for participating employees.
Unlike the standard Employment Injury and Invalidity schemes, employers do not share the cost of the Lindung 24 Jam contribution.
How much are you actually paying every month?
To put this into perspective, here is how much an employee would contribute at selected salary levels.
The standard First Category contribution is shared between employers and employees, while the additional Lindung 24 Jam contribution is borne entirely by employees who participate in the scheme.
https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30885188/
These figures follow Socso’s published Phase One contribution schedule. They exclude the Employment Insurance System (EIS), which is a separate contribution.
For local employees who do not participate in Lindung 24 Jam, the employee contribution is the standard Invalidity Scheme share shown in the table.
Employees can use Socso’s online contribution calculator to check their applicable contributions.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
For employment-related accidents, employers are generally responsible for reporting the incident to Socso by submitting an Accident Report, known as Borang 34. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
How do you make a Socso claim?
If you are involved in a workplace accident or suffer an injury while commuting to work, you should inform your employer as soon as possible.
For employment-related accidents, employers are generally responsible for reporting the incident to Socso by submitting an Accident Report, known as Borang 34.
Supporting documents include:
A copy of the employee’s identification card.
Medical certificates or documents relating to the injury.
Attendance records or time cards.
10dd1d36af4191ae: DHAKA, Nov 16 — Unions representing Bangladeshi garment manufacturers threatened on
Saturday to walk away from wage negotiations and shut factories indefinitely if protesters kept vandalising them during demonstrations for higher pay.

Bangladesh is the world’s second-largest garment exporter after China, producing clothes for major international brands like Fruit of the Loom, Levi Strauss and VF Corp, whose labels include Vans, Timberland and The North Face.
Worker unrest over wages began in October and has occasionally turned violent, with demonstrators torching police vehicles and damaging property during clashes this month.

The two main manufacturing unions – the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) – sharpened their rhetoric on Saturday.

“BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected,” BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said at a news briefing in the capital Dhaka.
“If the situation persists, we must reconsider,” Khan said.
“Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh’s labour law,” he added.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Garment workers rally in Dhaka on November 13, 2026 demanding a US$260 (RM982) minimum wage. — NurPhoto pic via AFP
The “no work, no pay” provision of Bangladesh labour law allows factory owners to suspend operations without paying workers.
Workers say rising food, housing, transport and healthcare costs have eroded their purchasing power in a country where inflation is running at around eight per cent.
Shutdown notices
They are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka (US$240; RM982) — a 140-per cent increase on the current 12,500 taka (RM409).

The protests have threatened to disrupt an industry that earns around US$38 billion (RM155.4 billion) annually, accounting for four-fifths of Bangladesh’s export earnings and employing more than four million workers.

More than 4,500 factories are registered with trade bodies like the BGMEA.
Workers staged fresh demonstrations in Gazipur on Saturday, blocking traffic for more than an hour before they were dispersed by law enforcement officers.
Managers at some of the dozens of closed factories in Ashulia posted notices announcing indefinite shutdowns.
Mazharul Islam, general manager of S-21 Apparels Limited, said a group of workers had disrupted operations despite most employees reporting for duty.

Bangladesh border guards patrol a street outside a textile factory in Dhaka on November 14, 2026, amid garment workers’ protests for higher pay. — AFP pic
“Around 95 per cent of workers came to work as usual on Thursday morning, while a few angry workers started shouting and forcing others to leave the factory,” he said.
“They vandalised the facility, and we had to announce its closure to protect the factory.”
The disruption comes during the run-up to Christmas, the busiest export period for Bangladesh’s garment industry.
“Due to the war (in Middle East), it takes an additional 10 days for shipments to reach their destinations, and now with this unrest... the sector is surely under threat,” Islam said.

a0d54ff8902f4b11: TAIWAN, Nov 16 — Indigenous farmer Banu Ismahasan walks through a golden field of tall stalks in southeastern Taiwan, harvesting by hand the grain heads of an ancient crop resistant to extreme weather.
Once grown by Indigenous farmers in Taiwan in case their staple crops died, oil millet largely disappeared from fields more than 60 years ago as rice became more available.

Over the past decade, Ismahasan and his elderly parents have worked to revive the nearly forgotten crop in the Bunun community in Buklavu, a village surrounded by lush green mountains in Taitung county.
“We just hope to bring back many traditional Bunun crops and grow them on this land again,” Ismahasan, 48, told AFP in his oil millet field under a clear blue sky.
Oil millet, or “dill” in the Bunun language, is endemic to Taiwan and can be found growing wild in the mountains.

Ismahasan first read about the plant online and then embarked on his own research, combing through historical documents and speaking to tribal elders, including a woman who recalled last eating it half a century ago.
He discovered that Bunun farmers used to grow oil millet alongside their staple crop foxtail millet as a “back-up” when harvests failed or disasters hit.
After years of growing oil millet himself, Ismahasan came to understand why his ancestors relied on the crop.

A single oil millet seed can grow 15 to 20 panicles, or branching seed clusters, and the stems regenerate on their own, while foxtail millet typically grows one panicle per seed and must be sown again after being cut.
It has also proven hardier than foxtail millet when extreme weather or disease outbreaks have ravaged his 2.2-hectare (5.4-acre) farm.
During a drought several years ago that lasted more than 200 days, the oil millet “stayed bright green” while other crops withered, Ismahasan said.
Typhoons, floods and even a rust disease outbreak have not affected it either.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Taiwanese farmers Linkav Ismahasan (left) and Banu Ismahasan harvest oil millet in a field in Taitung on October 21, 2026. — AFP pic
Hsing Yue-ie, a retired professor from Taiwan’s Academia Sinica and an expert in plant genetics, first heard of oil millet 15 years ago at an international forum.
Unbeknownst to Hsing, specimens of Taiwan oil millet collected in the 1890s were sitting in Britain’s Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew.
Hsing led a research team to find oil millet in the mountains of southeastern Taiwan and began studying the little-known cereal.
She found that the seed’s protective wax coating enabled it to grow without irrigation, fertilisers or pesticides, even on poor-quality land.
Rich in oil, protein and minerals, it can be used for human and animal consumption, as well as for fuel.
“It’s naturally very efficient at using sunlight and water,” said Hsing.
“As for soil conditions, even in mountainous areas where the ground is full of large rocks, it can still grow very well.”
‘Very precious’
Ismahasan started his crop with one panicle of oil millet.
The family now harvests oil millet twice a year on a section of their property where they grow other traditional Bunun cereal crops.
Tiny and tasteless, oil millet can be used in porridge, steamed buns, bread and even popcorn.
But the family has struggled to convince other farmers to grow it because it is not yet commercially viable.
Oil millet is not only labour intensive but also significantly more expensive for consumers than rice, by far Taiwan’s most popular staple.

While the current market for oil millet is limited, Taiwan’s National Crop Germplasm Center sees value in preserving its seeds for the future, when climate change might force more farmers to consider growing the crop.
Oil millet seeds are “very precious” because of their genetic diversity and ability to adapt to the environment, Lin Yen-yu, an assistant researcher at the centre, told AFP.
Seeds are kept in aluminium foil packets and stored at -18C under low-moisture conditions where they can last for decades, Lin said.
“In the future, when cultivation methods or climate change undergo certain shifts, their value may start to be recognised and discovered,” he said.
“It preserves many possibilities.”
Ismahasan said his priority for now was to get more people in his community growing and eating oil millet, bringing “it back into our everyday lives, just as it was for our elders”.
“If we don’t even eat it ourselves anymore, how can we expect to turn it into a viable business?” he said. — AFP
4e3b3836efc8ff88: From Hisham Aziz

The corporate anxieties following the tabling of Budget 2027 prompt a critical question: when did Malaysia’s apex industry associations transform from champions of free-market resilience into professional victims of helplessness?
The press releases and policy papers issued by the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers (FMM) suffer from structural issues that expose their lack of analytical weight and credibility.

FMM’s press statements exhibit the distinct characteristics of automated text generation — relying heavily on template-driven headers, passive phrasing, and generic buzzword aggregation like “supply chain resilience” and “digital transformation” in place of plant-level operational data. This reliance on high-level abstraction obscures true empirical rigor.

Rather than presenting detailed microeconomic data, unit-cost offsets, or lead-time data, FMM’s advocacy frequently uses sweeping language backed by disproportionately small survey sample sizes to demand massive policy concessions like credit lines, grant facilities, and tax deferments.
To the public and policymakers, organisations like FMM present themselves as fragile, over-burdened entities teetering on the edge of ruin due to basic regulatory adjustments.

Yet, a glance at public policy performance reveals an entirely different reality. These bodies represent the primary beneficiaries of decades of state largesse — enjoying extensive energy subsidies, infrastructure support, and generous tax incentives.

Under Budget 2027, this patronage continues unabated with fresh financing facilities from Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) alongside a transitional exemption from the RM2,000 minimum wage threshold for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
Despite this comprehensive safety net, the lobbying apparatus remains ever unquenchable.

In October 2026, FMM publicly expressed deep disappointment, lamenting a “lack of support” for the manufacturing sector simply because the government did not grant their requested RM1.5 billion extra support package. The danger lies not just in this sense of entitlement, but in the dubious, lightweight methodologies used to justify it.

Consider the statistical acrobatics deployed to influence national economic policy. In June 2026, FMM issued sweeping, alarmist warnings about global supply chain shocks — specifically the impact of the Strait of Hormuz conflict on domestic oil prices and SME survival.
The data to back these massive macroeconomic warnings? A survey pool of exactly 196 companies (FMM Geopolitical Impact Survey, June 2026).
To suggest that a survey pool smaller than a single mid-size factory floor can accurately reflect the structural vulnerabilities of Malaysia’s entire SME sector is absurd.
Yet, it is precisely on the back of these minuscule data sets that case studies are built to demand more credit lines, heavier grants, and broad credit deferments from the taxpayer.

This audacity reaches its peak when looking at their tax advocacy. In their September 2026 Business Conditions Survey (1H2026) briefing, FMM aggressively pushed for a return to the Goods and Services Tax (GST) but demanded it be implemented at a rock-bottom introductory rate of 3.0% — down from the historic 6% floor.
According to FMM’s own polling, while 68% of respondents demanded a rate below 5%, a full 41% explicitly called for a 3% rate.

How peak industrial representatives can genuinely look at Malaysia’s expanding national expenditure and rising infrastructure commitments and suggest halving consumption tax revenues is a great wonder.
They demand that public tax collection be gutted for their operational convenience, while simultaneously expecting the public purse to keep funding their multi-billion-ringgit economic safety nets.
FMM’s platform runs completely counter to the Madani government’s explicit agenda to transition Malaysia away from its unhealthy dependency on low-cost, low-skilled migrant labour.
By fighting tooth and nail against statutory wage floors and basic family protections, FMM is actively working to keep Malaysian wages artificially suppressed.
This short-sighted resistance eliminates the exact economic pressure businesses need to innovate.

If labour is kept artificially cheap through state exemptions and structural suppression, manufacturing firms will feel zero urgency to invest in research and development (R&D), upgrade their technology, or pursue genuine, automation-led productivity growth.
It is not possible to build an Industry 4.0 economy on an automated AI-generated script that begs to preserve an Industry 2.0 labour pool.
This irony peaks when looking at how FMM constructs its internal narratives.
In that same 1H2026 Survey, FMM dedicated an entire section to aggressively policing government administration, using curated survey questions to put HRD Corp in a distinctly negative light.

FMM explicitly complained that HRD Corp’s revised e-TRiS grant conditions actively “hindered training and planning” for 44% of businesses, highlighting that rigid bureaucratic rules — like the mandatory 14-day advance approval window — made it nearly impossible to provide urgent training.

FMM will meticulously poll its members to complain about public sector administrative flexibility, and they will rightfully demand accountability following HRD Corp’s financial mismanagement scandals.

Yet, they weaponize these administrative hurdles as a convenient shield to demand that training funds remain entirely under corporate autonomy. We see this exact transactional morality in their response to parental benefits.

While FMM aggressively fought the statutory 98-day maternity leave mandate as an unbearable operational cost when forced to pay for it, they happily celebrate the newly proposed Budget 2027 post-maternity allowance simply because the state is funding it through the Employment Insurance System (EIS).

They expect national tax revenues to be minimised and public funding maximised whenever it protects their corporate ledger but completely reject socioeconomic flexibility when asked to internally finance a liveable wage or grant a recovering mother an extra month of leave.
The government must stop treating these large corporate blocks as fragile patients in need of permanent economic life support.
True economic restructuring requires rigorous data, authentic feedback, and shared sacrifice. Not fake narratives and political manipulation.
Policymakers should look past the AI-generated statements and reports based on questionable methodologies and unreliable sample sizes and look closely at the empirical reality.

Malaysia’s industrial sector is well-capitalised and heavily subsidised. It is time they scaled up through innovation, automation, and R&D, rather than lobbying their way out of basic social contracts.
Malaysia’s manufacturing cannot be on permanent life-support to pander to a small group of people, nor held ransom by people using trade associations for their political agenda.
Hisham Aziz is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

Stranded passengers wandered through chaotic US airports for a third day.
Officials blame Friday's huge snafu on faulty work to upgrade air traffic control communication cables.
President Donald Trump on Sunday ended uncharacteristic days of silence on the ground stop, but only to blame his predecessor Joe Biden for the debacle.

Trump insisted he inherited a mess from the Biden administration and said Congress, which his party has controlled for two years, must approve funds to upgrade America's outdated air traffic control system.
"The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster," Trump said, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration.
"Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began," Trump asserted.
FAA chief Bryan Bedford had said Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans stranded at airports would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday.
However, transportation secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday morning it will actually take longer to get planes, crews and travellers to where they need to be.
"So, in the airspace, we're going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow," Duffy said on ABC News.
"We had airplanes and crews out of position because of Friday, so it takes a little bit of time to do that," he said.
'I'm the secretary'

Duffy also flatly rejected calls for his resignation over the travel chaos, insisting he inherited woefully outdated air traffic control infrastructure, such as, he said, radar equipment that dates back to the 1960s.
"So when we do work and things go wrong, of course I'm the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me," Duffy said in an interview on CNN.
As of Sunday afternoon, more than 1,880 flights within, into or out of the US had been cancelled, according to the travel monitor site FlightAware.
The Trump administration has blamed Friday's ground stoppage - meaning no planes can take off - on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines.
Friday's disruption was only the second time such a ground stop had been issued in US airspace, which is among the busiest in the world, since the 9/11 attacks.
The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos, it also raised serious concerns about the country's aging infrastructure.

Duffy has appealed for US$50 billion in funds to upgrade and modernise the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to "meet this moment".

8a6b39297448afa6: From Sadiq Asyraf

When Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi left the hall at the Melaka International Trade Centre on Saturday night, he was not sent off with a victory song. Barisan Nasional supporters chanted one word, over and over: "Bubar!" Dissolve.

Umno still sits in the unity coalition government, and its president is one of the two deputy prime ministers. But since September, BN has said it will leave the government the moment Parliament is dissolved.

Spontaneous or not, the chant fits Umno's position all year, which might be called minimum loyalty: do exactly what the coalition agreement requires and nothing more. That lets Umno push the government towards the edge without pulling it down itself.
Minimum loyalty

Umno information chief Azalina Othman Said set out the limits the day before polling. On her reading, the agreement obliges Umno to back the prime minister only on confidence votes, supply bills and procedural motions touching the government's legitimacy. Beyond that, Umno is free to disagree.

That reading covers Umno's conduct this year: going solo in Johor, partnering Perikatan Nasional in Negeri Sembilan and Melaka, and defending the conditional pardon of former prime minister Najib Razak against DAP's objections. All of it sits within the letter of the agreement.
Umno supplies just enough votes to keep the government standing while campaigning against its partners in the states. The unity government now rests more on seat arithmetic than on trust.

Azalina answered DAP's call for Umno ministers to resign with four options: mediate, stay calm, end the agreement, or review the clause on Islam, the Malays and the Rulers at the risk of unpredictable consequences.

With no termination clause in the agreement, Azalina presented dissolution as the logical political outcome. But ending a coalition agreement does not, by itself, constitutionally require Parliament to be dissolved. The next move, she told DAP, was theirs.
Read together, the options allow Umno to shift to Pakatan Harapan much of the immediate political cost of a rupture.

On Tuesday, Zahid said he would rather see Parliament dissolved than the Cabinet reshuffled. On Thursday, after DAP's challenge, he said BN still backed Anwar Ibrahim federally. On Saturday, his victory press conference spoke of a hattrick and, according to media reports, not of dissolution. About 40 minutes later, his supporters at the MITC entrance said it for him.

Unless the leadership distances itself from the chant, it is one message sent through two channels. Agenda-setting theory explains why the second channel matters: the media may not decide what audiences think, but they shape what audiences think about. Supporters filmed and shared the "Bubar!" clips themselves.

The likely effect is to shift attention from BN's victory in a state contest to the stability of the federal government. The question of the week becomes when Parliament will be dissolved, and it is the prime minister, rather than Umno, who is pressed to answer it.

PH plays the same game. Two nights before polling, Anwar quipped that some government critics sat beside him in Cabinet, then said he was not targeting Zahid. The same night, defending DAP, he asked whether it was DAP that had been responsible for the problems at Tabung Haji, Felda and 1MDB, a pointed reference to administrations led by his own federal partner.
After the results, he offered congratulations and cooperation. Both partners campaign against each other, then make up on paper.
The dissolution trap

Melaka gave the dissolution push its evidence. According to official results, BN won 21 seats, PN three and PH four, all of them urban DAP seats. BN matched its 2021 tally, and the combined BN and PN vote share barely moved, at about 63%.

The difference is that BN and PN no longer split their votes by contesting against one another. PH's share fell from 35.7 to 29.3%. Its candidates in Ayer Limau and Serkam lost their deposits with less than 12% of the vote.
That shifts bargaining power: PH has struggled to demonstrate electoral strength in Malay-majority constituencies, while Umno remains the government's principal Malay political partner.

The strategy has limits. PN won three of its five allotted seats, including Bukit Katil from PH. Outside government, Umno would face the same PN partners for Malay-majority seats at GE16 without the advantages of office.

Minimum loyalty pays best while Umno is inside the government. That creates a strong incentive for Umno to let PH initiate any rupture, so that it can present itself as the party that honoured the agreement until the end.

For Anwar, every exit has a price. Dissolving now means facing BN and PN together at PH's weakest point, after setbacks in Sabah, Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka. Holding on lets Umno enjoy power in Putrajaya while building the story of a government clinging to office.

Some DAP supporters want Umno ministers sacked. Whether the government could survive without BN's MPs depends on parliamentary arithmetic that has shifted this year. But the case for keeping Umno is political as much as numerical: it is the government's principal Malay political partner. Melaka suggests that value is under strain, and sacking Umno would simply set it free.
Whatever Anwar decides, minimum loyalty gives Umno a ready story. Sacked, it leaves as the betrayed partner. If Parliament is dissolved, it is merely keeping its promise to the king.

The unity government may yet be reshaped or run its full term. But if the partnership does break, the contest that matters will be over who controls the story of the separation. On Saturday night, Umno's supporters showed they intend to write the first draft.
Sadiq Asyraf is a political communication and media warfare analyst.

283e267e00a3ace8: WASHINGTON: US air travel is not expected to return to normal schedules until late on Sunday, the head of the FAA said, as the aviation system gradually recovers from a nationwide flight shutdown that officials blamed on routine maintenance gone awry.

As of 9.35pm ET (0235 GMT), airlines on Saturday had cancelled more than 6,400 US flights and delayed more than 8,000, according to FlightAware, an aviation website. That followed about 9,200 flights cancelled and 7,500 delayed on Friday after the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop because of disruptions to air traffic communications. FlightAware said 875 flights scheduled for Sunday were already cancelled.

Federal Aviation Administration head Bryan Bedford said on Saturday that he expected airline operations to largely return to normal by late Sunday. He also apologised for the disruption, adding that the system remains stable.

The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours. It was the longest nationwide halt to air travel since the attacks of Sept 11, 2001, and one of the single worst US travel days ever.

The issue prompted the White House to convene an emergency meeting in the Situation Room on Friday and federal agencies to scramble to determine if it was a cyberattack. But the problem was traced to FAA contractor L3Harris' installation of at least one new router at a remote facility, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday.

"We're working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was," Duffy said at a press conference.

The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, a union representing FAA safety employees, said the issue was isolated to two routers that were updated Friday. An official told Reuters it was believed the routers were in Arkansas and Texas.
An FAA official said the agency conducted a safety assessment before the work. The union said PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.
L3Harris said it took the issue seriously and is supporting the FAA in its investigation. Its shares last traded down about four per cent after hours on Friday.
OVERLOADED COMMUNICATIONS CENTRES

Duffy said the trouble began on Friday afternoon, when air traffic control centres experienced instability in radar and communications systems. The router issue led to data overloading other communications centres, officials said.

"We had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, and what that did was (it) gave us issues with our communication with aeroplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar," Duffy added.

The issue affected communications at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centres, which control aircraft during the cruise portion of a flight. Bedford said the FAA ordered the ground stop in case a centre lost all communications. "No facilities went dark. Nothing was fully lost," Bedford added.
The FAA said it was doing additional testing with L3Harris to see if there are any additional risks.

Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines all cancelled about 25 per cent of their flights on Saturday, while JetBlue cancelled nearly 45 per cent. Airlines have issued travel waivers allowing passengers to rebook flights for later dates without cost.

Though the FAA lifted the ground stop on Friday evening, the disruption for passengers was far from over, with tens of thousands of people stranded in airports. Airlines were trying to get flight crews and other personnel in position to resume flights.
The disruption stranded some college football teams on Friday before games scheduled for Saturday.
FUNDS SOUGHT TO FIX SYSTEM STRAIN

Friday's disruption is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by aging technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.
Duffy called on Friday for US$50 billion in funding to upgrade air traffic control systems, up from his earlier request of US$30 billion — after Congress approved US$12.5 billion last year.

House Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News on Saturday that he supports approving more funding for air traffic this year. Johnson's Republicans control Congress until next year, when Democrats will take over because of their gains in the Nov 3 midterm elections.

US Representatives Rick Larsen and Andre Carson, Democrats slated next year to chair the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and aviation subcommittee, respectively, said in a joint statement Saturday that their panels will "hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again."

That's the issue explored in Inside Gaza, a new documentary that follows journalists from global news agency AFP who were trapped in the territory as Israel exacted a fearsome revenge for Hamas' Oct 7 attack.

Director Helene Lam Trong brings these news industry veterans in front of the camera, showing how they balance the difficult task of reporting on the massive military response with their own survival, as it destroys their city, killing family, friends and colleagues.

"Most international correspondents... cover a war or a news event and then return home to safety," said freelance journalist and documentary filmmaker Lam Trong in Los Angeles, where the film was shown as part of The American French Film Festival.
"Palestinian journalists could not do that. They were trapped alongside the civilian population of Gaza, with no way out; as the days passed, they themselves became victims of the war."
The Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct 7, 2023, killed more than 1,200 people, the vast majority of them civilians. Armed men also took more than 200 people hostage.
Israel almost immediately sealed the borders of the Gaza Strip and barred international journalists from entering.

It then launched an enormous military response, pulverising swathes of Gaza in attacks that have left 73,000 people dead, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

Unable to send a team of reinforcements, AFP was solely dependent on the work of its local staff — experienced reporters, photographers and videojournalists, many of whom have worked internationally — to document Gaza's subsequent descent into violence and despair.
Without journalists like these, whose work was transmitted to AFP's thousands of media clients, the outside world would have had no idea what was happening inside Gaza, said Lam Trong.

In the film, which was compiled from material produced by the team on the ground, as well as from interviews conducted after they finally left, the journalists speak of the frustration of seeing their work either called into question or simply never broadcast or published.
In one sequence, the team describes their frustration at the way in which Israeli propagandists claimed genuine photos of a dead child were staged using a doll.
"At AFP, our photos, news reports and videos are used by world media outlets. But in this war, some of our images were never used," says Gaza bureau chief Adel Zaanoun.
"It worried us, even terrified us, because from the very first days, the thousand of Palestinians killed didn't count for the media."

At a time of declining engagement for traditional journalism as audiences migrate to unmoderated social media platforms and politicians seek to demonise any outlet publishing stories they do not like, Lam Trong says it is vital the public understands how newsgathering works — including the costs and the risks to those who do it.
That includes becoming targets themselves. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists and Reporters Without Borders, approximately 200 journalists have died in Gaza since the war began.
AFP's office in Gaza, which was broadcasting a live feed to clients, was hit, likely by Israeli tank fire, according to an investigation by the agency and other international media outlets.

"In Gaza, in particular, journalism and journalists have become central issues, as they have been killed, attacked and persecuted," said Lam Trong. "We do not deserve to be accused of propaganda when we conduct on-the-ground reporting."

Lam Trong, a recipient of the Albert Londres Prize — often described as the French equivalent of the Pulitzer — hopes the film, which has won numerous international awards and is eligible for Oscar contention, will spread the message of the importance of journalism.

The awards season campaign is "an opportunity to bring a very important message to Hollywood... that freedom of the press is under threat and that we must defend journalists — not just journalism, but the journalists themselves".
AFP's staff left Gaza in 2024. The agency continues its impartial coverage of the region using trusted freelance contributors.

0d640906b57b72dd: Lethal autonomous weapons powered by artificial intelligence (AI) are set to revolutionise warfare, but there is no proper regulatory or legal framework governing the new technology.
A conference starting today at the United Nations in Geneva will discuss how to establish curbs and prohibitions on such weapons, called killer robots by some.
But some analysts doubt the discussions at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons will keep pace with the fast-changing weapons.

Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) "can identify, select and engage a target without the intervention of a human operator in the execution of these tasks", said Geneva Centre for Security Policy head of global and emerging risks Jean-Marc Rickli.
Autonomous weapons have long existed.

An anti-personnel mine "is an autonomous weapon in the sense that it explodes when someone steps on it", said Laure de Roucy-Rochegonde of the Centre for Geopolitics of Technology at the French Institute of International Relations.

But with the proliferation of AI-enhanced drones, such weapons are now "capable of selecting and engaging a target that was not predetermined, adapting to their environment without human intervention", said Rickli.
So the critical issue for potential regulators lies in determining the level of human control over the decision to employ such a weapon.
The United States refers to an "appropriate levels of human judgment" in the use of autonomous weapons.
France maintains that a human must remain in the decision-making loop and bans LAWS, but permits "partially autonomous" systems known as PLAWS.

"The human role is always ensured through what is termed 'appropriate control' by a military commander — a concept that varies in scope depending on the system's criticality and the operational context," said Rear Admiral Vincent Sebastien, deputy director of the French Defence Ministry's Agency for Defence Artificial Intelligence.

"We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: the autonomous targeting of humans by machines," UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres and International Committee of the Red Cross president Mirjana Spoljaric warned in a joint statement in August.
But analysts said the Geneva discussions, while important, will touch only part of the issue.
Today, the diminishing role of humans is being driven by the growing use of AI in analysis and targeting.
Rickli said the scope of the agenda in Geneva is "very narrow".
"It fails to encompass the full range of issues surrounding AI on the battlefield" — an area where its use is expanding, particularly in target generation.
He said this was seen in the US-Israeli war against Iran this year "where the Americans engaged as many as 1,000 targets per day" inside Iran.
"There are a host of problems and unacceptable risks associated with targeting and decision-support systems," added de Roucy-Rochegonde.

"What kind of human supervision is required to ensure that the operator is genuinely exercising their own judgment rather than simply providing a rubber stamp for the machine's recommendations?" she asked.

The autonomous weapons to be discussed in Geneva are not yet in widespread use, although analysts have noted that they have been deployed by Russia in its invasion of Ukraine as well as US attacks in Iran.
But the spread is inevitable.
"Autonomy will very quickly become a reality on the battlefield," warned Sebastien.
"Autonomous weapon systems are not part of a distant future—a race towards greater autonomy in weapons systems is already well underway," said Guterres and Spoljaric in their statement.

Yet significant doubts and dangers remain, Dario Amodei, head of the AI giant Anthropic, warned this year: "Today, frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons."
But ultimately, the incentive for major powers is too strong.
Swarms of autonomous drones would be highly effective and some states view them as a crucial strategic advantage, said Rickli.
In January, the Chinese Defence Ministry described swarms of autonomous drones as the "new face of warfare".

"In an era of sharp military competition, the first state to normalise fully autonomous lethal strikes will reset expectations for everyone else," said Gerald Mako, a research affiliate of Cambridge University in the Small Wars Journal.

4f250e9dc2b671a5: As most analysts predicted, Barisan Nasional's electoral understanding with Perikatan Nasional helped it secure an even stronger mandate in the just-concluded Melaka election.

This election offers another illustration of how the political landscape has undergone considerable changes in recent years, with traditional rivalries increasingly giving way to political cooperation and coalition-building.
BN and PN setting aside their differences to contest under a common electoral arrangement would have been difficult to imagine when both coalitions were competing fiercely for political dominance.
The nation's increasingly fragmented political landscape in recent years has made such cooperation more important, even vital, for long-term national political stability.
This is as it should be. Long-term political well-being for the country demands that responsible political groupings think outside the box with the end of rigid political boundaries.
Traditional rivalries may be making way for increasing political pragmatism all round, as parties show willingness to work with opponents as and when circumstances demand it.

Our political landscape has always demanded that political parties and their leaders appreciate coalition-building as a necessity. Negotiations and compromises are critical to make coalitions workable and durable.
This goes to show that politics as the art of the possible — which worked so well for half a century since Merdeka — is not lost on our current generation of leaders.

That said, the electorate deserves the utmost respect and regard. It expects and should get consistency and clarity. Parties must explain how their alliances reconcile with their previously-held positions and principles.
Voters should not be left guessing as to what they are actually endorsing. Flushed with overwhelming victories, coalitions may understandably want to savour their electoral honeymoons.
But they must never forget that the real test comes after elections.

Coalition-building and political compromises may work fine at the theoretical level; now comes the harder part, putting all that into practice and showing voters that a new partnership works for and in their interests.
If there is something that never goes out of fashion in Malaysia, it is political moderation in governance.
The nation has gone through thick and thin by practising the art of compromise which requires moderation, not just in views and utterances but through actions and policy implementation.
Each political alliance will need to demonstrate that it can function as an effective governing arrangement rather than simply an electoral compact that delivers the votes and wins legislative seats.
The business of government is not always headline-grabbing. In fact, it may be more about ensuring the necessary rules and laws are in place and seeing to it that they work well in everyday practice.

60ce259d5f318b29: KUALA LUMPUR: Tun Hakim Tun Hasnul Azam came agonisingly close to pulling off a dramatic victory at the Asian Tenpin Bowling Championships in Doha, Qatar, on Sunday, only for a stubborn 10-pin to end his hopes of men's singles gold.
The Malaysian had to settle for silver with 1,383 pins, just seven short of Kuwait's Abdulrazzaq Mohammad, who had set the winning mark of 1,390 in Saturday's opening squad.
Hakim, competing in the second squad, appeared well on course to overhaul the Kuwaiti's total after accumulating 970 pins in his first four games.
He needed just 420 pins from his remaining two games to draw level, but his challenge hit a snag when he managed only 165 in the fifth.
That left him needing a massive 255 in his final game to force a tie, setting the stage for a thrilling finish.
Hakim refused to surrender and took his gold-medal chase all the way to the bonus 11th frame, where he needed a strike to keep his hopes alive.
But the 10th pin stood, leaving him to finish with 248 and settle for silver, just two pins ahead of Hong Kong's bronze medallist Michael Mak (1,381).
"Of course, being just seven pins away from gold is a tough one to take. It was such a close finish, and looking back, there were definitely a few shots I could have executed better," said Hakim.
"But overall, I'm proud of the way I competed and gave it my best until the very last frame."
Hakim attributed his costly fifth game to difficulties adapting to changing lane conditions.
"I had a good run going in the first four games, but in Game 5, I struggled a little with the lane transition.
"I couldn't quite get the reaction I wanted and lost some momentum. At this level, every shot counts, and unfortunately, that game made the difference."
Despite the setback, Hakim showed tremendous fighting spirit to give himself one last shot at gold.
"I knew I still had a chance, so I just tried to reset mentally and focus on one shot at a time.
"I made some adjustments, trusted my game plan, and stayed committed to every shot. I'm happy I managed to finish strong and put myself back in contention for gold."
The silver was nevertheless another significant addition to Hakim's Asian Championships collection, taking his career haul to eight medals across four editions.
It was also his first singles medal, bringing his overall tally to two gold, three silver and three bronze medals.
Hakim previously helped Malaysia capture the team gold in Hong Kong in 2023 before winning the doubles title alongside Shaqeem Izwan Teh in Bangkok two years ago.
He was also part of the Malaysian team who narrowly missed out on gold in Bangkok, losing to Singapore by just 26 pins.
That disappointment remains fresh in his mind, with Hakim stressing that reclaiming the team title is Malaysia's main priority in Doha.
"Singles event is a bonus," said Hakim, who emphasised that the team gold remains the main target..
"I think it's a bit of both. As an athlete, you always compete to win, especially when you're representing your country.
"But at the same time, a silver medal is still something to be proud of. I'll take the positives from this performance, learn from the mistakes, and keep moving forward."
Hakim's silver was Malaysia's second medal in Doha following Gillian Lim's women's singles triumph on Saturday.
Defending men's singles champion Rafiq Ismail narrowly missed the podium, finishing sixth with 1,377 pins, just four short of bronze.
Hazim Alihanafiah placed seventh (1,367), followed by Izz Naqiuddin Putera in 13th (1,331), Timmy Tan in 28th (1,284) and Syafiq Ridhwan in 43rd (1,255).
With Malaysia collecting a gold and silver from the opening singles events, Hakim believes the defending overall champions have made an encouraging start.
"I think it's a really positive start for Team Malaysia, and hopefully we can carry this momentum into the remaining events," he said.

"We have a strong team with plenty of experience and talent. But we also know the competition is tough, so the most important thing is to stay focused, support each other, and take it one event at a time."

6f34bdccb710b683: Dave Maass has been writing about comics for more than 20 years, and now he also writes comics. By day, he teaches tech investigative techniques at the University of Nevada, Reno Reynolds School of Journalism and researches surveillance at the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

If I was the manager of a comic book store, I’d create a section for “journalism nerdcore.” It’s where I would stock Transmetropolitan, DMZ, and Abbott–comics that place fictional journalists in the center of genre stories, be it science fiction, action or horror. Despite their daylight jobs, Spider-Man and Superman wouldn’t be allowed there, but DC’s Lois Lane would find a home of her own.

On the end-of-shelf display, with a big fat, Sharpie-written “Employee Pick of 2026” sign: Exploit, the new comic series from Laura Hudson and Tim Leong and illustrator Emiliana Pinna, which was just published last month by Mad Cave Studios in its collected trade paperback volume. It doesn’t get more journalism nerdcore than its tag line: “Don’t Bury The Lede. Bury Your Enemies!”

Exploit is an action thriller inspired by the battle raging right now between the tech oligarchy and the independent press. Editorial intern Kirby Kuo is trying to score her first byline in RIOT!, a WIRED-style print magazine, before the newsroom is wiped out by its soon-to-be new owner, a thin-skinned Alex Karp-flavored cyberlibertarian-turned-technofascist. But when the subject of her reporting is assassinated on a live stream, Kirby finds herself facing the blame, on the run and forced to place her trust in agoraphobic hacker Lenox and Cold War-alum cybermercenary Ipsum.

Creators Hudson and Leong shared the masthead at WIRED (senior editor and director of digital design, respectively), but long before that they ran Comic Foundry, where they were “the team that changed comics journalism forever,” as ComicsBeat put it. Their careers have dovetailed between comics and journalism for years, with Hudson putting time at The Verge and ComicsAlliance and logging bylines in The Guardian, The New York Times, and Slate, and Leong holding creative roles at Fortune and Entertainment Weekly, while also writing and designing the Super Graphic series.

All that experience shows. Between the chase sequences and heist-planning, there are plot points based on real episodes in tech and cybersecurity uncovered in publications like 404 Media, WIRED, and The Markup. But the panels radiate with the earnest love for scrappy, independent journalism–especially print journalism–and a molten fury for those who threaten it.
I asked Hudson some questions to learn more about the heart and rage she poured into this series. The following has been edited for length and to avoid spoilers.
Dave Maass: Comics love an origin story. Take me through the back story of Exploit.

Laura Hudson: We've been working on Exploit since we met up in a diner in LA in 2019, pre-pandemic. I don't live in LA but I was there working on a TV show, and it was the first time we'd lived in the same city since mid-aughts New York. Tim fucking LOVES print, and we'd both spent the last decade watching print journalism collapse from the inside. There are definitely scenes in the comic, and a few darlings we had to cut, that were ripped directly from real life whether anyone believes us or not. We arrived just after the good times had ended, in time to hear all the stories about how amazing it had been, and watch it get worse and worse. And of course, the generation just after us only experiences the wreckage.

Tim had an idea for a comic set at a print magazine in New York, and I started imagining how I would feel, starting out as a journalist now. It always makes me think of donut blocks, from Super Mario Bros 3 on. They're the round, cakey-looking blocks in the game that start shaking when you step on them, and then fall down. So if you're going to walk across them, you better run, or you're gonna die. If you stop, you're gonna die. So, you can't stop. Ever. I understand that feeling intimately, and I knew I could write from there. And hell, I've wanted to make comics for over 30 years and now I'm finally doing it at 45? Fuck me.

Exploit’s main protagonist is a journalist (technically an intern) working for a magazine that specializes in tech investigations. It’s a WIRED meets Mother Jones kind of affair, but also if VICE’s Motherboard had been a standalone, hard-copy publication. Why choose a tech journalist as your hero?

It probably says something about me that this question baffles me. Maybe I've just known too many good tech journalists, because to me it feels so obvious. Technology and the internet have played, are playing, and will play transformative roles in our lives, often in ways that few people fully understand. We're still governed by a gerontocracy where many of our leaders conceptualize the internet as a bewildering series of tubes, possibly now filled with AI. Our technology has surpassed our ability to legislate it or address it ethically to such an extreme degree that some tech leaders are actually asking to be stopped. The internet (or at least its infrastructure) is a hyperobject in the Mortonian sense of the word, something so massive, complex and distributed that people struggle to comprehend it fully. We can see pieces of it, and effects of it, but it's impossible to perceive or experience it as a whole, even and especially when we are inside it.

But as Morton has written in reference to climate change, apocalyptic framing around hyperobjects can lead to hopelessness and inaction in situations when things genuinely can be addressed: "You are closing down the future. You are making your reader submit to tyrannical despair." Recognizing the enormity of something, in both the classic and popular sense, doesn't have to mean giving up. People who refuse to accept that something is too vast, too complicated, or too powerful to challenge are pretty compelling to me. That's what the best tech journalists do.

Now let’s talk about the dual villains–both techbro executives at a start-up that is not only a government contractor, but aims to take over key government functions. Now the last comparable comic I read like this was 2014’s Hacktivist (written by of all people actor Alyssa Milano with Jackson Lanzing and Collin Kelly), and it also featured two very similar tech bros–but they were the heroes, moonlighting as digital freedom fighters. That was a time where people were inspired by larger-than-life figures like Jack Dorsey and Elon Musk. That's not so much the case anymore. How would you say that Exploit’s antagonists reflect the shift in the public perception, and activities, of the “founder” class in our society?

We want to believe that there is someone coming to save us, and since billionaires were the ones powerful enough to fuck up human civilization, it makes sense that we'd look for someone of equal power to save us. It makes sense to want that. But this is a fairytale we tell ourselves, which I say as someone who once wanted to believe it was at least possible. But no one is coming to save us. Let me say it one more time, because this is important: NO ONE IS COMING TO SAVE US. Billionaires least of all. Tech billionaires, by and large, are much better at destroying than fixing, and have advertised this fact for decades. They like to move fast and break things, and leave them broken. Many of them struggle to understand human beings socially even as they run social networks. They are prone to massive ego, can have anything they want at any time, and exist in bubble worlds where they are never told no.

These are the people we're putting in charge of the future? I wouldn't put them in charge of a Dairy Queen. And I personally believe that some of them would be willing to accept the deaths of millions or even billions of people as the cost of advancing humanity in whatever sci-fi way they have imagined. Their obscene wealth requires them to exist at a scope that most humans are not built for, like images stretched out over miles. It distorts them as individuals, and it can distort their morality, insofar as it ever existed beyond the desire to advance and profit. This has become more evident as more tech leaders have chosen to behave as open buffoons in an age of buffoonery. But this is who they always were.

From the first pages of the book, we’re introduced to the very real, extreme asymmetrical conflict between tech billionaires. Even a poorly paid journalist can threaten a billionaire (or at least his ego), but a billionaire has so much money, it’s easy to crush a publication. It immediately made me think of Jeff Bezos buying the Washington Post, Peter Thiel bankrolling the attacks on Gawker, and cases where surveillance companies have threatened news outlets. Am I wrong to think that’s the overarching theme of the whole series?

Nope. I feel an anger about it so deep that I almost intuitively dissociate when it comes up. Not because I don't think I should be angry, but because I have learned I cannot be angry all the time without deleterious effects. Sometimes you just have to play the Yakety-Sax song in your head until the feeling passes, because you have to get things done today. It's worth noting that Kirby and Lenox (and Ipsum) [Note: Lenox is a young hacker and Ipsum is an old-school cybermercenary] undertake their mission with full knowledge that it will probably ruin their lives. That's part of the benefit package of being a billionaire. People can't challenge you without possibly ruining their lives.

Now Exploit isn’t meant to be a realistic treatment of tech journalism, but I do think there’s a lot of truth in how you portray the perils faced by journalists who deal with hackers and leakers. This is running in a publication that specializes in that, but a lot of other journalists have been burned pretty bad, some even ending up in jail. How did reality affect the way you handled the relationship between your protagonist and the various hackers who enter her orbit?

We've all seen things go very wrong for journalists, even those who meant well. Kirby has lived more life than the average intern, and done some journalistic work, but never at this level and never with these kinds of sources. She's green, and we wanted to show that. Before the big lead comes in, we have her pitching stories from sources that clearly have their own agenda, and her pitches get slapped down. That kind of pushback is essential, and what helps you learn before you're in a position to make serious mistakes. Kirby is pushed into a very big story before she is probably ready, but she's the only one in a position to do it. We wanted it to be clear that she's able to do what she does not just because she's smart and brave, but because she has an experienced group around her.

Dealing with hackers, leakers, and sensitive sources requires dealing with two competing impulses as a journalist. Good journalism requires rigorous skepticism as a discipline. There's that journo saying that if your mother says she loves you, check it out. But developing a relationship with a source requires trust on both sides, and risk on both sides. One of the things Kirby learns is that a source is not necessarily an ally, even when they have valuable information. Their goals may overlap in places, but they can be different in invisible and dangerous ways. It's not something anyone should approach lightly or without care.

A quarter of the way into the book, you introduce an assassination drone–and I initially expected it to be a sort of “Chekhov’s gun” that would play a huge role later on. But, it actually wasn’t. It turned out the most frightening thing still is people–specifically the mobs of doxxers who worship tech demagogues. Does this mirror your own experiences with online harassment?

One of the things people used to say a lot, to dismiss or ignore the nightmarish world of online harassment, is that it was "only" online. You could just close your computer and go outside, so really, wasn't it all in your head? This line of convenient fiction collapsed pretty quickly, as doxxing, swatting, stalking, assaulting, raping, and molesting people through the internet became, shall we say, super popular? You can't dismiss the internet as a fake, unreal place where nothing of consequence matters. We know it matters now, that it's dangerous. But now it almost feels too late to care. These systems and the people who run them have certainly shown they don't care, and there's no Band-Aid you can put on it now to fix it. We could have built the internet and its social architecture very differently, in a way that prioritized dialogue over the right to abuse. But the trolls thought it was funny, and the companies wanted more money, so here we are living in the cursed labyrinth of their lols.

One thing about an assassination drone, though: everyone understands it as a weapon. A tool of sorts, but one designed explicitly to cause damage. Its goals and impacts are not opaque. Social media platforms were pitched as a way to connect people, to give them the power to reach out and touch anyone from anywhere. Giving this power away to anyone who wanted it with little to no accountability was described by tech companies at the time as inherently good. It took longer—some would say too long—for everyone to realize the scope of the damage it could cause. Or that this incredible communications technology could double as a custom-made playground for grifters, bullies and predators of every stripe. So yeah, people are the scary part. But people get a lot scarier when they are given great power with zero accountability.

Zines play a major plot point in the book. But you also made a promotional zine for San Diego Comic-Con, which included a lot of digital security advice. How do you see physical media reemerging in political life?

Tim designed that, by the way, and I can't believe how much it looks like an actual riot grrrl zine. Zines have long been linked to comics culture, and you can see the overlap in a lot of indie comics spaces and events. But zines—or as they once called them, pamphlets—have been powerful political tools for over 500 years. They have defeated churches and kings. And they're a very compelling tool right now, as a form of dissent that exists outside of the internet and its platforms. You can't hack a printed page. And we don't think about it this way anymore, but writing on paper is a communications technology—perhaps the greatest in the history of the world—and we should regard it as such. A lot of obsolete or antiquated tech can have value today because accessibility is also vulnerability, and obsolescence is its own kind of security feature. There are some impressive Gen Z zine enthusiasts, and a great WIRED article about the scene. But I'd love to see more people pick up that torch, for both creative and political reasons. No one can stop you.
What do you hope people will take away from Exploit? How do you hope it will make them feel?

In the year of our Lord 2026, I would be happy just to give people a bit of distraction from the horrors. But if you feel like your life has been suffused by the feeling that you showed up after the party was over, and that it's only downhill from here, then we made this, in part, for you. It's a grim feeling we know well, a sort of miasmic dread that flattens the future and makes you feel helpless and paralyzed. And that's exactly how a lot of terrible people want you to feel. They want you to lie down and allow the terrible machine to function smoothly around you. Both Kirby and Lenox come up with their own imperfect coping mechanisms for that reality and feeling, but they do cope. They do move forward and fight, and they don't do it alone. They can't, and neither can we.
957e051c57a8639c: SONGKHLA: Three Malaysian tourists were fined a total of 12,000 baht (about RM1,447) by Thai police after they were caught obstructing traffic and making illegal vehicle modifications along Phetkasem Road in Hat Yai early today.

Hat Yai Police Station deputy traffic inspector Police Lieutenant Prut Pattanapran said the three men, aged between 26 and 30, were summoned to the police station along with a Thai national following public complaints about their conduct.
He said the incident occurred at 12.30am and involved three Malaysian-registered cars, in blue, red and white, and a black car belonging to the Thai national, travelling in a convoy along the road.

"The driver of the black car at the front was believed to be recording a video for social media content, while the group of vehicles made several U-turns, revved their engines loudly and obstructed traffic," he told reporters today.
Prut said their actions angered local residents before footage of the incident went viral on social media.
"The group of tourists was believed to have been recording social media content while carrying out these stunts and may not have been aware of Thailand's traffic regulations," he said.
He said all four individuals pleaded guilty and paid fines of 4,000 baht (about RM482) each before being released today.
Prut advised foreign tourists to understand, respect and comply with Thai laws throughout their stay to avoid breaking the law.

11154fe8c15cf1a2: SINGAPORE, Nov 15 — Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed International, under scrutiny for allegedly steering Nvidia chips to China, said on Sunday that suspected spy Alice Huang had left the firm more than a year ago.
Megaspeed is suspected of helping Chinese firms get around US export controls by buying Nvidia chips for its data centres in South-east Asia and routing them to China.

Its former director Alice Huang has been identified in US media as an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who had a relationship with Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned as the tech giant’s chief executive on Thursday.
“Ms Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the company,” the firm said in reply to an AFP query.
“Megaspeed does not comment on Ms Huang’s personal and private matters.”
Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are not related.
Beijing has denied the spying allegations.
Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a November 8 letter to Nvidia employees that did not name the woman involved.
Nvidia’s board has said it will investigate the matter, and three US Congress committee chairs have asked Jensen Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on November 18.

Megaspeed said it “conducts legitimate and lawful business”, and that it was aware of media reports “containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence”.

The tech group also said it has retained an external legal counsel “to conduct a thorough internal investigation” of its compliance obligations under US export control laws, which limit the transfer of some advanced chips to China.

Singapore authorities said servers containing advanced AI chips were being exported to Malaysia and were suspected of being delivered to other destinations, contrary to declarations made in the city-state.
Investigations into Megaspeed “are ongoing”, Singapore’s police force has said.
Authorities also said they had barred Alice Huang in February from re-entering the city-state after she provided inaccurate information during a probe into Megaspeed.
She was not, however, investigated for espionage. — AFP
