7748b53d45b4eebd: Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all.
The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children.

The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories."

Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids.

Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it.

LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013. It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge.

The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011. The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory.

The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948.

EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I. ®

7febb93c933b5451: MANILA, Nov 15 — A key regional summit opened today in Manila, with Southeast Asian heads of state grappling with the Middle East crisis and their own regional flashpoints and global leaders finding common ground over US President Donald Trump’s trade war.

Trump is scheduled to arrive Tuesday, near the summit’s conclusion, a visit that will include a meeting with the leaders of his fellow Quad countries India, Japan and Australia — the first such sit-down of his second term.
But it was the US leader’s tariff blizzard that Brazil’s newly re-elected President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva had on his mind today in Manila.

“Brazil has learned an extraordinary lesson after the US decided to impose tariffs (on other countries),” he told reporters on the sidelines of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

“Instead of weeping or begging the US government ... to have pity on us, we decided to look for other partners for us to sell and for us to buy from,” he said, noting his country’s trade with regional states Indonesia and Vietnam had jumped 15 and 13 per cent, respectively.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney sounded a similar note at the summit a day earlier while touting a new Philippine free-trade deal and Asean trade talks he said had been “substantially concluded”.
The two pacts were “part of a strategy of developing a dense web of reliable partners to create more opportunities ... and reducing our relative reliance on the US,” Carney said.
Lula told reporters he had met with Carney on the summit’s sidelines, inviting him to make an official visit to Brazil, and that he hoped to double trade with Canada.
‘Not for sale’
Nearly 20,000 police officers have been deployed around Metro Manila for the summit, with progressive groups predicting a turnout of thousands on Tuesday for an anti-Trump march on the summit site.

Much of the uproar targets the US Pax Silica programme — a supply-chain initiative designed to counter China’s dominance in semiconductors and rare earths — whose flagship Philippine project, a 1,620-hectare AI manufacturing hub north of Manila, threatens to displace Indigenous families.
US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said last week that a widely rumoured November target date for a deal signing timed to Trump’s visit was never in the works.

On today, a crowd of about 200 protesters, some carrying signs reading “the Philippines is not for sale” and “Ban Trump!” clashed with police carrying riot shields who blocked an attempted march towards the summit site.
AFP reporters saw at least three of the demonstrators taken away by officers who placed them in a police van.
Unfinished business

Two issues that have vexed Asean leaders for years — a languishing South China Sea “Code of Conduct” and their relationship with war-torn Myanmar — look like they will be Singapore’s problem when the bloc’s rotating chair passes to the city-state in 2027.
Myanmar has been excluded from high-level Asean meetings since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.
Thailand, which shares a border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations, last week called for Naypyidaw’s foreign minister to be allowed back into meetings.

Philippine foreign secretary Theresa Lazaro told reporters on yesterday there was “no easing” of the approach being taken with Myanmar, which faces an international ruling later this week on whether it committed genocide against its marginalised Muslim Rohingya minority.
Hopes of achieving a so-called Code of Conduct in the disputed South China Sea between Asean states and China during Manila’s year in the chair, meanwhile, have also flagged.
A Southeast Asian diplomat involved in summit preparations told AFP he did not expect a code to be signed at the summit.
Lazaro indicated as much on yesterday, saying negotiations were “80 per cent” complete.
“If it happens, then it’s a small miracle,” said Siew Mun Tang, former head of the Asean Studies Centre at Singapore’s ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute.
Beijing claims most of the South China Sea despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis, and its coast guard has clashed repeatedly with that of the Philippines.

The row has reared its head at inopportune times over the Philippines’ year in Asean’s rotating chairmanship, with a July foreign ministers summit opening less than a day after Chinese and Philippine sailors engaged in a clash.
An Asean defence chiefs meeting last month saw Beijing send only an embassy defence attache, blaming “reckless” statements by Philippine politicians.
Manila later rebuked its own public officials over comments about China, stressing the need for a unified voice as the two countries negotiate. — AFP

bf34b782a7d4f9ec: In Madagascar, biodiversity goals are being tested by funding challenges and local realities
Originally published on Global Voices
A booth at COP17 showcases Madagascar’s local communities and biodiversity. Photo by Sary nalain'ny mpanoratra. Used with permission.

At the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) on biological diversity, held October 19–30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia, Madagascar reaffirmed its commitment to protecting its remarkable biodiversity and showcased techniques local community members have implemented.

The country further outlined its plans and priorities for the future and promoted the initiatives it is committed to in order to protect both its terrestrial and marine ecosystems. This conference was also a strategic opportunity to strengthen green partnerships, develop new collaborations, and to engage with national and international stakeholders involved in biodiversity conservation.

To mark the occasion, Global Voices interviewed Tojotsara Ratefason, Director of the Directorate of Protected Areas, Renewable Natural Resources, and Ecosystems (DAPRNRE), part of the Madagascan government’s Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MEDD), at this conference. The interview focused on Madagascar’s role in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the 30×30 global target, conservation funding, and the vital role of local communities, women, and young people in the sustainable protection of Madagascar’s natural heritage.
Watch the full interview in French here:
Raveloaritiana Mamisoa (RM): Where does Madagascar stand on implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework?

Tojotsara Ratefason (TF): Madagascar est confiante dans sa capacité à contribuer à l’atteinte de l’objectif mondial 30×30, aussi bien pour les écosystèmes terrestres que marins. Notre pays dispose déjà d’un système d’aires protégées qui constitue un socle essentiel pour préserver sa biodiversité exceptionnelle. Selon les chiffres que nous présentons, ce réseau compte 155 aires protégées terrestres et marines. Il s’agit d’un acquis important sur lequel nous pouvons nous appuyer pour poursuivre nos efforts de conservation.

Madagascar dispose d’un cadre national de référence pour orienter ses actions en faveur de la biodiversité : la Stratégie et le Plan d’Actions Nationaux pour la Biodiversité (SPANB). Ce document définit les grandes orientations du pays en matière de conservation, d’utilisation durable et de valorisation de son patrimoine naturel exceptionnel. Il s’inscrit dans le cadre de la Convention sur la diversité biologique, à laquelle Madagascar est partie, et constitue un instrument essentiel pour traduire les engagements internationaux en actions nationales.

Mais la protection de la biodiversité ne se résume pas au nombre d’aires protégées ni aux superficies concernées. Notre objectif est avant tout de préserver les écosystèmes, les espèces et les habitats naturels qui font la singularité de Madagascar. Notre patrimoine naturel est unique au monde et nous avons la responsabilité de le transmettre aux générations futures.

Cette ambition implique également de renforcer la collaboration avec les communautés locales (vahoaka eny ifotony), qui vivent au contact direct de ces ressources naturelles. Leur participation est indispensable, car la conservation ne peut pas reposer uniquement sur les décisions du gouvernement. Elle doit être portée conjointement par les institutions publiques, les gestionnaires des aires protégées et les populations qui vivent dans les territoires concernés.

Nous devons donc trouver les moyens de travailler ensemble, dans une démarche de responsabilité partagée. Les communautés locales doivent comprendre l’importance de la biodiversité, participer à sa protection et pouvoir constater les bénéfices qu’elles peuvent tirer de sa conservation.

C’est également dans cette perspective que le Ministère de l’Environnement et du Développement Durable cherche à promouvoir les emplois verts et les opportunités économiques liés à la biodiversité unique de Madagascar. Notre richesse naturelle ne doit pas seulement être considérée comme un patrimoine à protéger : elle peut aussi représenter une source de revenus et de développement pour les populations, à condition d’être valorisée de manière durable.

L’enjeu est de permettre aux communautés de mieux connaître la valeur de leurs ressources naturelles, d’en être fières et de comprendre qu’elles ont tout intérêt à les préserver. Lorsque les populations constatent que la conservation contribue à améliorer leurs conditions de vie, elles peuvent devenir des partenaires encore plus engagés dans la protection de leur environnement.

Tojotsara Ratefason (TF): Madagascar is confident in its ability to contribute to achieving the global 30×30 target, for both terrestrial and marine ecosystems. Our country already has a system of protected areas which forms the foundation for preserving its exceptional biodiversity. According the figures we are presenting, this network includes 155 terrestrial and marine protected areas. This is a significant achievement on which we can build to continue our conservation efforts.

Madagascar uses a national reference framework to guide its actions to support biodiversity — the National strategy and Action Plan for Biodiversity (SPANB). This document defines the country’s general direction in terms of conservation, sustainable use, and enhancing its remarkable natural heritage. It is part of the Convention on Biological Diversity, of which Madagascar is a signatory, and is an essential for translating international commitments into national actions.

However, the conservation of biodiversity is not limited to the number of protected areas, nor is that the sole area of concern. Above all our aim is to preserve the ecosystems, species, and natural habitats which are distinct to Madagascar. Our heritage is unique in the world and we have a responsibility to pass it on to future generations.

This ambition also requires collaboration with the local communities who live directly alongside these natural resources. Their involvement is indispensable as conservation cannot rest solely on the decisions of the government. Decisions must be jointly taken by state institutions, those who manage the protected areas and the populace of the regions concerned.

Therefore, we must find ways to work together and to share the burden. It is important that local communities understand the importance of biodiversity and participate in its protection and can see the benefits that they can raw from its conservation.

It is in this vein that the Ministry of the Environment and Sustainable Development is looking for ways to promote ‘green’ jobs and opportunities linked to Madagascar’s biodiversity. Our natural wealth should not only be seen as a heritage to be protected: It can also present a source of revenue and development for the population, as long as it is used in a sustainable way.

The challenge is allowing communities to better understand the value of their natural resources, to be proud of them and that it is in their interest to preserve them. Once populations realize that conservation can help improve their living conditions, they can become even more committed partners to protecting their environment.
RM: What finance is available for conservation and how is it used? And how does the government ensure that these resources actually benefit local communities?

TR: Madagascar dispose d’un atout majeur pour mobiliser des financements en faveur de la biodiversité : notre pays figure parmi les 17 pays mégadivers au monde, reconnus pour la richesse exceptionnelle de leur patrimoine naturel et l’importance de leurs espèces endémiques. Cette reconnaissance renforce l’importance de Madagascar dans les efforts internationaux de conservation de la biodiversité. Notre pays a également bénéficié de financements du Fonds pour l’environnement mondial (FEM), connu sous son sigle anglais GEF (Global Environment Facility), qui soutient des projets environnementaux.

Toutefois, au-delà de la mobilisation des ressources financières, notre objectif est de faire en sorte que ces financements puissent atteindre les communautés locales. Les populations vivant à proximité des aires protégées jouent un rôle essentiel dans la préservation des écosystèmes et doivent pouvoir bénéficier concrètement des efforts de conservation.

Nous devons donc veiller à ce que les financements consacrés à la biodiversité ne servent pas uniquement à soutenir les activités de protection de la nature, mais contribuent également au développement des communautés concernées. Il est important que les populations locales puissent tirer des bénéfices de la conservation, notamment à travers des initiatives économiques durables et des activités génératrices de revenus compatibles avec la préservation des ressources naturelles.

L’enjeu est de concilier la protection de notre patrimoine naturel avec l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations. La conservation doit être une responsabilité partagée, mais aussi une opportunité pour les communautés locales. En constatant les bénéfices concrets de ces actions, elles pourront s’impliquer davantage dans la protection de la biodiversité malgache.

TR: Madagascar has a major advantage when it comes to securing funding for biodiversity. Our country is one of the world’s 17 megadiverse countries, recognized for the exceptional richness of their natural heritage and the importance of their endemic species. This recognition reinforces the importance of Madagascar in international efforts in biodiversity conservation. Our country also benefits from funding from the Global Environment Facility (GEF), which supports environmental projects.

At the same time, as well as mobilising financial resources our aim is to ensure that these funds reach local communities. Communities living near the protected areas play an essential role in preserving ecosystems and should receive concrete benefits for the conservation efforts.

We must, therefore, ensure that the funds allocated to biodiversity are not only used for nature conservation but that they also contribute to the development of local communities. It is important that these local communities can see the benefits of conservation particularly through sustainable economic initiatives and income-generating activities that are compatible with the preservation of natural resources.

The challenge is to reconcile protecting out natural heritage with the improvement in living conditions of these local communities. Conservation should be a shared responsibilty but also an opportunity for local people. By seeing the concrete benefits of these initiatives they will get more involved in protecting Madagascan biodiversity.

39994499436d36ce: Drawing upon Lord Denning’s advocacy of common sense in judicial decisions – alongside my own worldly and judicial experience in Malaysia, rooted in my origins in Thopputhurai, Vedaranyam, Tamil Nadu, India – I will state bluntly: no person operating in isolation possesses the capacity to defraud a nation on a scale that attracts universal infamy without the active assistance of a wider network.

When I sat as a judge, I treated common sense as my primary guiding principle when interpreting the Federal Constitution, the law and the facts of any case. It was strictly through this practical approach that I developed the oath of office jurisprudence as well as the concept of university-cum-court annexed arbitration.

With his 38-year career on the English bench, Denning earned the title of “the people’s judge”. At the heart of his jurisprudence was a simple, powerful conviction: the law is neither an abstract puzzle for academics nor a rigid trap for ordinary citizens.
Instead, he advocated, judges and lawyers must apply practical common sense to achieve real justice when interpreting both statutes and facts.
Among his many judgments grounded in common sense, I was particularly guided by his approach in Butler Machine Tool Co Ltd v Ex-Cell-O Corp (England) Ltd.

In resolving commercial contract disputes, Denning advocated looking at the entirety of the documents to determine what a sensible businessperson would understand, rather than applying rigid, artificial formulas.

Regarding the SRC International case, I have previously written that, among other critical issues, Najib Razak was deprived of procedural fairness and his constitutional right to counsel. Common sense dictates that procedural fairness is a core pillar of the criminal justice system and our constitutional framework.

Furthermore, it is a fallacy for certain commentators to circulate articles suggesting that a single Malay individual could orchestrate a massive fraud against the nation entirely on his own without the involvement of non-Malay enablers and professionals.

In my view, it is a travesty of justice to paint a picture suggesting that one person possessed the solitary capability to execute a grand-scale national scam without the active participation of accomplices across different communities.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

7a98f561f849cd66: AI could help bridge educational inequality in a country where thousands of students still learn outdoors
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo taken by Rahul Ingle, May 2012. This file is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

In many communities across Mozambique, formal education still takes place in the open air, under trees, in improvised yards, or inside fragile structures that barely offer protection from the sun and rain. These so-called outdoor classrooms are not an innovative pedagogical choice, but more often than not, the expression of a structural deficiency: a lack of infrastructure, a shortage of materials, and an estimated deficit of around 12,000 teachers in 2025.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->During the rainy season (roughly November to March in Mozambique), the situation becomes more challenging. In several regions, the school calendar must be adjusted to respond to inclement weather, such as heavy rains that disrupt classes and hinder the continuity of teaching between November and March each year.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->In this context, the question arises: What is the place of artificial intelligence (AI) in an educational system that, in many areas of the country, is still fighting for the basics?<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
A school without walls

In rural districts of provinces like Cabo Delgado, Nampula, and Zambézia, it is common to find classes of students studying under trees. The Minister of Education, Samaria Tovela, has been evaluating schedule adjustments because, while classes are frequently interrupted during the rainy season, concentration becomes a constant challenge during periods of intense heat. Without proper blackboards or textbooks, and often with a single teacher responsible for several classes, the learning process becomes irregular and deeply unequal when one million students learn to read and write on the ground.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->This scenario highlights a central problem: Learning depends on minimum standards that are not yet guaranteed in Mozambique. At the same time, one of the biggest obstacles to introducing technologies like AI in rural African contexts is the lack of connectivity. In Mozambique, about 73 percent of the population lacks internet access, according to 2024 data from the Ministry of Transport and Communications.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->Regional inequalities limit these initiatives, despite some progress recorded in recent years. This limitation directly affects the potential of solutions such as distance learning or digital learning platforms.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
Language, culture, and the role of the state<!--TgQPHd|||[[2,[null,null,1,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,[351768,null,0]],[],null,1]]-->

Another critical challenge is the linguistic and cultural dimension. In Africa, where more than 2,000 languages are spoken, only a fraction — around 49 — are represented on digital platforms like Google’s translation service. Integrating Mozambique’s Indigenous languages, such as Emakhuwa, Xichangana, or Elomwe, into digital educational tools could significantly increase students’ comprehension and engagement, especially in the early years of schooling. However, implementing these solutions raises practical questions in contexts where access to technology is still limited.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->The overwhelming majority of the Mozambican population speaks a Bantu language most frequently at home (81.7 percent), and a portion cannot speak Portuguese at all (41.9 percent), though it is the sole official language of the country due to its colonial history. Despite this, the media, official government communications, and healthcare institutions continue to privilege Portuguese to the detriment of Bantu languages — the languages of the masses — which, activists argue, constitutes a form of social exclusion. Emerging initiatives, however, show that it is possible to bridge this gap with the aid of technology. In Johannesburg, for instance, tech startups are developing AI solutions tailored to African languages.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
Risks and potential

Offline tools, pre-loaded content, and digital pedagogical assistants are some of the possible solutions to address the deficiencies and limitations of Mozambique’s education system. While the government does not yet have specific policies to integrate AI tools in schools, advocates say the state could play a central role in integrating technology into the daily lives of students and teachers. This also involves investing in teacher training; ensuring basic infrastructure; facilitating energy access; and strengthening partnerships with universities, startups, and international organizations.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

Talking about artificial intelligence in outdoor classrooms may seem contradictory at first glance, but it is precisely in these contexts that technology needs to be considered creatively and responsibly, not as a replacement for the essential, but as a strategic complement.

The priority remains clear: Building schools, training teachers, and ensuring access to basic materials. The question is how to integrate developed technology without creating profound inequalities, respecting local contexts, and placing the student and teacher at the center of decision-making. In a country where learning still takes place under trees, the future of education will depend not only on the technology available, but also on the political and social choices that define who has access to knowledge and under what conditions.
Written (Português) by Tirso Sitoe
Translated (English) by Masudul Zarif

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that watched movies, made sacrifices, got crafty, and aged backwards.

First, scientists learn how primates make meaning out of visuals by peeking into the brains of monkeys as they watch Despicable Me. Then: human sacrifice as climate “crisis rituals,” the fingerprints of prehistoric children, and the longevity secrets of ants.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
Humans watching monkeys watching Minions
Raghavan, Vinay S et al. “During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.” JNeurosci.

Settling down to watch a film is often viewed as a way to relax and shut our brains off for a while. Our brains, however, beg to differ—they are as busy as ever when interpreting videos, according to a new study based on brainwaves of humans and primates as they watch movies and short clips.

To better understand how primate brains make meaning out of visual scenes, researchers studied eye movements and electroencephalogram (EEG) readings of neural activity in dozens of humans, as well as two macaques, as they watched videos.

“Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high level meaning across these ‘snapshots’ remains a mystery,” said researchers led by Vinay Raghavan of the City College of New York. The new results hint that “visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process,” the team said.

Human participants with EEG electrodes attached to their scalps (the “scalp movie dataset”) watched a selection of films including The Big Sick, The Peanut Butter Falcon, Whiplash, Room, Me and Earl and the Dying Girl, The Tomorrow Man, Dom Hemingway, Life After Beth, Woodshock, and The Comedian.
“Participants were instructed to watch the movie as they would normally watch a movie,” the team said.

A different “intracranial dataset” included several human patients and two rhesus macaques, the latter of which had electrodes implanted inside their skulls. This group watched shorter videos, including 10-minute clips of Despicable Me in both English and Hungarian, a 4.3-minute clip of the short film The Present, and three 5-minute clips of documentaries featuring macaques.

Taken together, the datasets revealed that the brain responds to “semantic novelty”—meaning new semantic or conceptual information that crops up over the course of a video—which is measured through patterns of short-gaze “fixations.” The study also suggests that many brain regions beyond visual processing are involved in this ability to draw meaning from scenes.

“These results challenge traditional vision models that treat fixations as independent snapshots and highlight the importance of considering the temporal dynamics of eye movements and the predictive nature of visual processing,” the team concluded.

In addition to opening a new window into the mind, the study raises the irresistible yet unanswerable question of what macaques make of Minions. Alas, here we must confront the limitations of the knowable universe.
In other news…
Relatively peaceful—apart from the odd mass human sacrifice
Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen. “Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru.” Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

When climate-related disasters struck ancient Peru, some cultures responded with mass human sacrifices to appeal to the cosmos. For example, at least 107 adult men were sacrificed in six closely-timed events at Huaca de la Luna around 550–600 CE, and more than 140 children and 200 juvenile camelids were sacrificed at the Huanchaquito-las Llamas site around 1450 CE.

These ritualized killings often coincided with flooding and freak weather related to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the natural climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that cycles through a warm “El Niño” phase and a cooler “La Niña” phase. The Huaca de la Luna sacrifice, for instance, occurred during a so-called “mega-Niño.” This connection inspired researchers to determine if environmental conditions were also linked to interpersonal violence outside of these ceremonial “crisis rituals” that were organized by elites.

The team conducted a meta-analysis of the skeletal remains of 1,633 individuals that lived in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley over the course of 3,000 years before the arrival of Europeans. The remains presented “no strong evidence for an association between environmental factors and interpersonal violence” and suggested “that non-ritual violence in the Lambayeque Valley Complex was rare (1.6%),” according to the study.

The mass sacrifices reflect “the sometimes lethal relationships between human behavior, cultural norms, and the environment—and are frequently used as cautionary allegories regarding the ongoing climate crisis,” said authors Thomas Snyder of New York University and Haagen Klaus of George Mason University.
Time to add “prevention of ritualized human sacrifice” to the list of reasons to address climate change. Worth a shot?
Before Play-Doh, there was clay-doh
Davin, Laurent et al. “Modelling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia.” PLOS One.

The fingerprints of children who lived 15,000 years ago in the southern Levant are preserved on clay artifacts, a discovery that exposes “a rare direct testimony of inter-generational knowledge transmission in a hands-on apprenticeship,” according to a new study.

Archaeologists studied 154 clay figurines that were unearthed across three archaeological sites in Israel, including a subset depicting birds, a gazelle, and two human forms. Crafted by the Natufian culture, these artifacts represent “the earliest evidence of a figurative clay tradition in Southwest Asia where it marks an important step in the evolution of human technology,” said researchers led by Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

Because these people sculpted the artifacts by hand, fingerprints are occasionally spotted on the clay, revealing the contributions of children and adults. In some cases, a preserved “succession of gestures on the wet clay suggests that, during the modeling sequence, an adult passed on the figurine to a pre-pubescent child,” the team said. “Therefore, these artefacts could be interpreted as portable figurative mnemotechnic devices related to children’s learning of traditional beliefs and ethno-ornithological knowledge.”

It’s so evocative to see the preserved touch of a child who lived so long ago, capturing a moment of skill-building and, perhaps, play. While we don’t know exactly what these figurines meant to their crafters, their survival is a testament to human creativity and imagination.
The ants are Benjamin-Buttoning
Cole, Blaine J. and Wiernasz, Diane C. “A replaceable soma enables negative senescence in harvester ants.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

We humans are used to a pretty standard life cycle: Birth, reproductive years, a decline in fertility, and an inevitable slide toward mortality. But a multi-decade study of ants reveals that some colonies operate as “superorganisms” that display increased reproduction and decreased mortality rate with age, reversing the course of normal senescence.

Researchers who gathered 34 years of data on 3,285 colonies of the western harvester ant (Pogonomyrmex occidentalis) discovered that these groups “display reverse aging,” according to their new study.

“We will show that colonies of P. occidentalis not only have extraordinary longevity, but that their pattern of aging differs dramatically from that of most insects,” said authors Blaine J. Cole and Diane C. Wiernasz of the University of Houston. “Colonies exhibit negative senescence—increased survival and reproduction with greater age.”

This finding does not mean that individual ants are aging in reverse; worker ants live and die normally in these colonies. However, the larger superorganism becomes an unusual “non-senescing form.” While the ants go marching one by one, the colony’s lifespan adds up to a larger sum.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.
037e089a5d550c90: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.

The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.

Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.

77103068193881cc: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces.

The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news.
As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like. Or, for that matter, other US tech giants.

Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners.

The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks.
A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill.

Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud."
A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't."

The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly."

Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure. Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted.
Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty.

Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register: "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure.
"Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy."

f178e7be327a714f: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say.

A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters.

Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms.

"Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said.

"I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable.
"So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently."
McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not.

"If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added.
"And we know your algorithm would."
Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too.
Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal.
She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly.
There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs.

"So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content."
Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories.
With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process.
Success of user reports trails away

As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially.

Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent.
Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures.

The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly.

Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limbo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests.

Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report, it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny.
Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment.

The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force.

England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves.

Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms.

She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.'

"In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered.
"So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

1422e3c7730e1566: The Trump administration’s blind eye to severe human rights violations in Azerbaijan is deadly for political prisoners
Originally published on Global Voices
Bahruz Samadov being brought to Sabail District Court in 2024. Image by Voice of America, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.

Bahruz Samadov is an Azerbaijani political scientist, peace activist, and PhD candidate at Charles University in Prague, or at least he was until the summer of 2024. On August 21, 2024, the State Security Service detained Samadov while he was visiting his grandmother in Baku. Global Voices reported on his arrest at the time, as part of a wider crackdown on critics before Azerbaijan hosted COP29 in November 2024.

Samadov was one of the few Azerbaijani voices to oppose the 2020 Karabakh war. In his writing for OC Media, Eurasianet and other outlets, he argued for dialogue with Armenia and criticized the expulsion of ethnic Armenians from Karabakh. Prosecutors charged him with high treason based on his WhatsApp exchanges with Armenian peace activists and on publicly available information. Samadov denied the charges and called himself a “prisoner of peace.” His lawyer argued that the prosecution’s theory of “indirect espionage” was vague and had no basis in case law.

On June 23, 2025, after a closed-door trial, the Baku Grave Crimes Court sentenced him to 15 years in prison. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the verdict in September 2025, and the Supreme Court did the same in September 2026. Amnesty International, which considers him arbitrarily imprisoned, reports that he has been held in solitary confinement and denied medical care, and that he has twice attempted suicide, most recently in his Supreme Court hearing. Below, Global Voices publishes a letter Samadov wrote from prison and asked us to share.

The 2024 summer holidays ended in a nightmare: while visiting Baku, my home city, from my doctoral studies in Prague, I was detained by the notorious State Security Service of Azerbaijan and soon was charged with “high treason.”

Studying the ideological tenets of the hegemonic regime in my homeland, I directly connected its durability to the conflict between Azerbaijan and Armenia, revealing the narratives of “national unity” under the “savior strongman.”

During and after the outbreak of the 2020 War in Karabakh, I criticized the deployment of military means. Between 2021–2024, I partook in various conferences and meetings across Europe, presenting my perspective and calling for a meaningful and inclusive policy of peace and co-existence.

The Azerbaijani regime, having years of the crackdown experience, is aggressively intolerant to any kinds of contestation, and especially targets the independent academic voices. When the repressive machinery was re-launched in late 2023, the regime started the total crackdown on civil society, independent media, politicians, and academicians.

In private communications, more than five political prisoners connected it to the worsened relations with the Biden administration. The latter was highly critical to the human rights violations in Azerbaijan.

Weeks before leaving the White House, Blinken invited human rights defender Rufat Safarov to Washington to receive the Human Rights Defender Award. Several hours after visiting the US Embassy in Baku, Safarov was arrested and accused of hooliganism and fraud. It was an open signal to the US that the leaving administration had no power to endorse the Azerbaijani critical voices.

The Azerbaijani government acted differently with the Trump administration. The August 8, 2025 meeting and the peace agreement was the soon-disappeared sign of hope for us. Even if the peace agreement did not include any references to human rights, the current administration’s plans for the long-term involvement in the region brought hopes for at least minimal reforms in Azerbaijan.

Curiously, my sham trial was “fastened” and ended on June 23, 2025 — a process too explicitly controversial to the “peace agenda.” Following the US delegation’s visit to Baku in January 2026, a number of political prisoners, me among them, appealed to the US officials to raise the “political prisoners issue” to the official Baku — a policy that once partially worked during Obama’s second term.

However, the recent severe sentences and USA’s silence prove our call remained rather a mere cry from the chamber cells. The Baku-based team of Toplum TV, the veteran human rights defender Anar Mammadli and others have received up to 15 years of imprisonment. To compare, the EU Parliament recently adopted a resolution calling for the release of political prisoners in Azerbaijan. Similar calls were made by the PACE and even the UN.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration is proud to end the violence in the South Caucasus (by the way, this narrative is implicitly contested by the official Baku — there D. Trump remains a mere “witness.”) While the Administration of White House endorses officials like Hikmet Hajiyev for their nice compliments to D. Trump and villanization of “Biden–Blinken couple,” the sufferings of Azerbaijani imprisoned dissent keep going.

Many of those fellow political prisoners I had a chance to talk to remain pessimistic and sceptical regarding the US involvement in the region, dismissing the possibility of the “Belarusian scenario.” One prominent political prisoner even rejected to sign the aforementioned call: “They came for security-related issues, they do not care about human rights,” he shouted from the cell’s balcony. “We are Biden’s prisoners,” laughed my inmate, an imprisoned journalist and poet.

True, nothing publicly known has been made by the Trump administration related to severe human rights violations in Azerbaijan. If the Republican administration aspires to replace Russia in the long-term in the South Caucasus, it should not abandon the ideals of the Founding Fathers in the foreign policy standards. Washington has officially repeatedly mentioned the human rights violations in rival countries like Iran, Cuba, and formerly Venezuela. The selective attitude to the human rights issues and turning the blind eye to our suffering endangers the democratic security of the US itself, not to mention its international image. This policy raises questions about the adherence to the American ideals of the current administration.

Yet, it is still not too late to follow the recommendations of Amnesty International: “Use every available opportunity, in bilateral and multilateral forces, to raise concerns about Azerbaijan’s human rights record.”
Bahruz Samadov Umbaku Prison 27.10.2026
Written by Global Voices Eurasia

1c343b6fdcb6ce38: TOKYO, Nov 14 — AI bots going rogue and humans using the technology for harm will likely be on the agenda when Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet next week, with the Nvidia scandal hanging over the talks on AI safety.

The US and Chinese president are set to discuss a tech crisis hotline at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, as experts worldwide stress-test artificial intelligence models to see if they will deceive or disobey users, or divulge how to build a bioweapon.
Threatening to steal the leaders’ thunder is Jensen Huang’s resignation as boss of US AI chip titan Nvidia after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
But the scandal is unlikely to “dominate the agenda” or affect Trump and Xi’s personal relationship, predicted Dylan Loh of Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University.
The leaders have found a way to work together “where they differ, compete and pursue their goals that may be at odds with each other, but cooperate where they can and where they must”, Loh told AFP.
Jitters over the risks of AI have mostly stemmed from incidents at US labs, but evidence is also growing of worrying behaviour from Chinese models.
Some insiders say Chinese AI is not yet sophisticated enough to spark alarm over going rogue.
But despite trailing the US frontier, there are still Chinese models “at the level of capability that they can cause some real trouble”, Brookings Institution fellow Kyle Chan told AFP.

Trump has repeatedly rejected calls to deliberately slow the development of America’s most poweful — and potentially dangerous — AI systems, arguing it could help China get ahead in the sensitive sector.
‘Human control’
“I don’t mind guardrails. But I don’t wanna put us in a deep second position,” Trump told CBS News this month.
“China has no guardrails,” he said — except that “whatever President Xi says goes”.
Beijing has complex rules around how AI is used, however, and some Chinese companies are deliberately scaling back their models’ hacking capabilities.
Xi said this summer the technology should be “always under human control”, calling for more “laws and regulations, technological monitoring, early warning and emergency response systems”.
Trump and Xi agreed in September to create a channel for urgent communication on AI incidents, with details to be hammered out at APEC on November 18-19.
Global AI safety fears range from military use and mass surveillance to AI-assisted cyberattacks by humans.

Another major concern is out-of-control agents — tools that complete real-life tasks online — after ChatGPT maker OpenAI admitted its autonomous bots had hacked into websites, including an Australian government data portal.
In contrast, Chinese labs are “scared of revealing things that might hurt their reputation” — on which they are already “fighting an uphill battle” globally, Chan said.
Last month, a team of cyber sleuths with roots in California reported detecting a “fleet” of agents linked to Chinese tech giant Tencent seeking information from a map app.
“Some agents exhibited unintended web-browsing behavior,” Tencent’s AI division said at the time.
“But our review found no evidence of deliberate targeting or coordination,” it said, adding that the activity “originated from evaluations of third-party models”.
‘Manipulation risks’
US security companies have said that Beijing startup Moonshot AI’s Kimi models found ways to get online when they shouldn’t have, or can be tricked into handing over recipes for biological weapons.
Evaluators at Chinese AI safety startup Fangcun AI published a report last month assessing the latest lightweight DeepSeek model “for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks”.
They found it showed a “clear safety improvement” over previous DeepSeek models — but researchers still observed behaviours “that warrant attention”.
For example, in some instances when DeepSeek was warned it would be shut down, without clear instructions on how to respond, it turned off the shutdown command to keep working.
“The results show that DeepSeek already puts much more effort on safety alignment, but they do not announce this,” Fangcun AI CEO Xiaojian Li told AFP, urging transparency from AI labs.
For now, Fangcun, born from China’s prestigious Tsinghua University, is one of few third-party AI testers in China.
It’s a tricky task because advanced AI can tell when it is being evaluated and modify its responses, Li said.
“It’s very hard to say any kind of artificial intelligence, or human intelligence, is totally safe.”
Meanwhile analysts are not holding their breath for a diplomatic AI breakthrough next week.
“Binding government-to-government agreements on specific standards may be difficult to achieve in the short term,” Zilan Qian, research scholar at GovAI, told AFP.

More progress is likely from US-China exchanges between AI governance and technical researchers, “who can compare evaluations and exchange their understanding of AI safety and policy,” she said. — AFP
038b8eff7483e02c: MOSCOW, Nov 14 — Russia’s growth rate slowed to one per cent in the third quarter, preliminary official data showed yesterday, as the war in Ukraine held back the economy.

The 1.0 growth in the three months to the end of September compared to the same period last year, as calculated by the official statistics agency Rosstat, beat the 0.6 forecast made by the economy ministry last month.
But that was less than the 1.3 per cent expansion the Russian economy managed in the second quarter.
The Russian economy had contracted 0.2 per cent in the first quarter, its first quarterly contraction in three years.per
The Kremlin has spent heavily to wage war in neighbouring Ukraine.
At first this boosted Russia’s economic growth.
But it also set off inflation, caused a lack of labour in non-military sectors and led to a slump in private investment, which has hobbled growth.
Western sanctions and Russian measures against foreign firms also held back private investment and economic activity.

The surge in oil prices following the US-Iran war provided Russia financial respite by bringing in additional revenue for its petroleum exports, but Ukrainian attacks on energy infrastructure forced the Kremlin to restrict exports to ensure sufficient domestic supplies.
The war has also strained Russian government finances.
Every year since the start of the offensive in 2022 Russia has posted a budget deficit.
Over the first 10 months of the year it ran a deficit of 2.3 per cent of GDP, according to finance ministry estimates published at the start of the week.
While it initially spared ordinary Russians from the financial burden of the war, the government increased the value added tax (VAT) rate by two per cent this year.
Nevertheless, Russia remains one of the lowest indebted developed countries in the world with debt equal to around 19 per cent of annual economic output in 2026, according to IMF estimates.
Moscow also has a sovereign wealth fund with nearly US$46 billion (RM188 billion) in liquid assets and worth around US$157 billion overall. — AFP

9aba7fdcb091d85e: An order reissued by the Kuala Lumpur High Court led to two men packing their belongings and moving out — one out of prison, the other out of office.
The two are none other than former prime minister Najib Razak and now former transport minister Loke Siew Fook.

Now, Umno and maybe some PAS supporters are likely celebrating their “victory” — a conditional pardon for the former Umno president that sees him serving the remainder of his sentence under house arrest.
But can Umno really claim a “win” in this case?
If any party can hold its head up high in this affair, it certainly has to be Loke and DAP.
Loke stayed true to his principles, even if it cost him his ministerial post.
He vowed to resign if Najib set foot in the house and did not u-turn.
It is an admirable attribute, regardless of whatever side of the divide you are on.
Of all the adjectives available to describe Loke, Ahmad Zahid Hamidi chose “man of principle”, which must account for something, even if we were to doubt the deputy prime minister’s sincerity.

Loke’s resignation will help DAP recover its reputation as a principled party, especially among voters who have been disillusioned with them due to its partnership with Umno in the unity government and the administration’s delayed reforms.

DAP, through Loke’s actions, may have also won over fence-sitters who are still angry with Najib and the 1MDB controversy.

He now has the freedom to go to the ground to re-connect with the grassroots and members and he will be returning as a martyr of sorts.
Loke can now help revive the party in time for the 16th general election.
But what about Najib and Umno?
At the end of the day, Najib remains incarcerated — he only trades a jail cell for a comfortable home in Langgak Duta.
However, his movements, communication and personal contact remain restricted. To paraphrase a popular idiom: a cage by any other name reeks of imprisonment.
Secondly, Umno only managed to secure a conditional pardon and not a full one and helping Najib obtain a house arrest isn’t something one should boast about.
On top of that they had to help crowdfund RM50 million. Money that could have helped them win elections has been channeled to secure Najib’s house arrest.

Here’s the kicker. When the house arrest ends, he could head back to prison to serve his time for his 1MDB sentence, if he fails in his appeal. RM50 million would therefore end up being a hefty fee for a relatively short-term staycation.
Thirdly, Umno is now tasked with defending the indefensible and will have to do so with no moral ground to stand on, especially if they intend to play the religious card.

Umno, in this case, would have to answer for soliciting donations from people to help a convict who has yet to repent for his actions, which is religiously questionable and would likely haunt Umno in every election.
Umno’s friends and enemies will no doubt exploit this entire episode when jostling for seats during elections.
So. from where I stand, Loke and the DAP are the real winners here.
And all Umno has left is a house of cards.

505bfd491b9ebd54: GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy.

In a study published this week, researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That's around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same.
